items.body:
Topdown Dialectic’s solo debut bow on False Aralia draws a line under over a decade of material in supremely elusive style & pattern - all rug-pulling rhythms and hallucinatory fractals wrapped up with proper, hyperreal frisson. Massive chef’s kiss FFO Vladislav Delay, Beatrice Dillon, Paperclip Minimiser, Purelink, Marc Leclair, T++.

An artist keenly observed since those initial anonymous gestures on /\\Aught in the early ‘10s, and through a cult LP trilogy for Peak Oil during 2018-2021; Topdown Dialectic has become a unique facet of C.21st dub electronics, adored for their grasp of diffused spatio-textural sorcery and wraithlike grooves. Anyone paying close attention to emergent sounds via Peak Oil and its False Aralia offshoot may have guessed at the project’s signature, watermarked imprint on the Borgesian Term EP of late ’25, which can now be confirmed as the work of one and the same Izaak Schlossmann; a photographer and producer patently in possession of heightened proprioceptions and a rewardingly patient approach to lushly dissociative sonification. In other words, he makes some of the sexiest electronic music out there - stuff that genuinely feels like it was made this century - and his latest practically leaves you kissing the sky thru its 80 minutes of lip-biting, skin tingling pressure. 

On 16 tracks timed at exactly 5 minutes each, we’re placed in the presence of suggestive sorcery in a unique ecology of oneiric physics. Never overtly showy or overblown, there’s nevertheless a staggering level of ingenuity and synaesthetic effect to its detailed construction and gaseous fractals resembling the LSD or DMT experience. The label themselves compare its nuance to “the flicker of a candle over a desk of drum machines in a Midwestern basement, or the “first blush of sunlight over a tiny campground as subwoofers creak in the distance”, which proves a perfectly poetic analog to its digitally-smudged refractions and tongue-tip spectral tumescence, and in effect feels like an aesthetic descendent of Torsten Pröfrock’s convulsive prototypes as T++. 

Ultimately, though, it’s a singular pleasure to immerse the senses in Topdown Dialectic’s self-contained soundsphere, and never more substantially so than on ‘False LP A’. Longtime enthusiasts will surely recognise his skill in parsing salient aspects of Basic Channel x Rhythm & Sound, and their descendants in Vladislav Delay or Pole, reframing those templates in far more uncertain space with a real animist magick. Each work feels tangibly, ambiguously alive, breathing with dynamics and more voluminous, macro scales, and iridescent with voices and details that commands attentive listeners who will have a field day zoning in/out to its illusive, holographic projections and syncopated chronics.
items._cn_summary: Topdown Dialectic在False Aralia旗下发行的首张个人专辑，以十六首各五分钟的曲目构成八十分钟的沉浸式声响场域。作品延续了其自2010年代初以来对扩散式空间纹理与幻影般律动的探索，将Basic Channel与Rhythm & Sound的遗产置入更不确定的声响维度中，形成一种类似致幻体验的气态分形结构。专辑的细节构造具有高度的精巧性与通感效果，节奏不断抽离又重组，声音仿佛在宏观与微观尺度间呼吸。乐评特别强调其数字模糊折射与感官张力，并关联至T++、Vladislav Delay等艺术家的脉络，但整体呈现出独立且鲜活的动感，值得专注聆听或放任意识游走。

items.album: The Remains: Short-Run Regional Releases from the Lao People's Democratic Republic
items.excerpt: Colour us enchanted with this otherworldly hour of airborne flute, Saw-U, vocal and drum spirits sourced from the night markets, museum shops and cafés of Laos, by Gary Sullivan ov Bodega Pop, who aptly compares them with Laurent Jeanneau’s forays in the same zone of interest for Akuphone & Sublime Frequencies. Check for the uncanny frissons of ‘Lam Cheung’ and its slew of piquant percussive works, all shimmering with the type of timeless lustre we’ve come to expect from Sullivan & DINTE’s magpi
items.body:
Colour us enchanted with this otherworldly hour of airborne flute, Saw-U, vocal and drum spirits sourced from the night markets, museum shops and cafés of Laos, by Gary Sullivan ov Bodega Pop, who aptly compares them with Laurent Jeanneau’s forays in the same zone of interest for Akuphone & Sublime Frequencies. Check for the uncanny frissons of ‘Lam Cheung’ and its slew of piquant percussive works, all shimmering with the type of timeless lustre we’ve come to expect from Sullivan & DINTE’s magpie picks...

"In Lao PDR, music was seemingly everywhere. Walking through an open field outside Savannakhet to the sound of someone playing a khaen on a distant porch, the bracing rush of electronic molam from of one of Vientiane’s many aging malls, the awkward blending of the blind so u player’s voice with the bustling sounds of Luang Prabang’s night market.

It was in that UNESCO World Heritage Site that I found most of the CDs and CD-Rs from which I’ve ripped the tracks for this compilation. I’m almost certain I picked up a thumb drive at the night market that held many hours of additional music that could have been included, but if so, I’ve misplaced it, lost it for good, or simply misremember purchasing it in the first place. What I do remember is that these discs were literally the last copies in the cafe, museum, bookstore, and night market where I bought them, and not all of them played all the way through without sonic deterioration.

The sounds compiled here play in stark contrast to the more contemporary recordings I found in Laos, most of which featured some form of upbeat digital workstation molam or children’s songs. In addition to the ever-present khaen, this collection includes recordings of the sanai, a single-reed instrument fashioned from a water buffalo horn, the ceremonial khong nyai gong, the pi and similar free-reeds, and at least a dozen more traditional instruments played by Lao and ethnic minority artists. While some of these tracks were laid down in Vientiane or Luang Prabang, most were recorded near where the artists lived, from the legendary Vat Phou in the far south to the former Pathet Lao capital Xam Neua in the northeast.

Unlike Laurent Jeanneau’s more focused Lao collections for Akuphone and Sublime Frequencies, which remain among my favorite albums of all time, the present cassette-only selection is literally all over the PDR map. The sequencing is entirely in response to rhythm and texture and includes recordings from the 1970s, 80s, 90s, and early aughts. This may frustrate those with more of an ethnomusicology bent, but my hope is that the listener experiences something akin to wandering for the first time through this majestic country, encountering the last copies of forgotten recordings one after another, and hearing in these remains fragments of the past and a living musical landscape."

–Gary Sullivan (Bodega Pop)”
items._genre: world music / traditional Lao / folk / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑由Bodega Pop的Gary Sullivan在老挝各地夜市、咖啡馆、博物馆和书店搜集而来，收录了1970年代至2000年代初的罕见CD与CD-R录音。音乐以传统老挝乐器为核心，包括笙（khaen）、水牛角单簧管（sanai）、仪式用孔艾锣（khong nyai）以及多种自由簧片乐器，演奏者多为老挝本土及少数民族艺术家。与Laurent Jeanneau更聚焦的录音不同，选曲按节奏与质感编排，而非民族音乐学逻辑，呈现一种漫游式的聆听体验，仿佛在陌生国度中逐一发现被遗忘的唱片残片。录音地点从南部的瓦普寺到东北部的前巴特寮首都桑怒，覆盖广泛，部分音质带有年代痕迹，却因此更显真实。整张合辑捕捉了老挝传统音乐景观中正在消逝的声响碎片，兼具档案价值与听觉魅力。

items.body:
The incomparable Winos dial-up a near-future fraught with glitching techno x surrealist folk artefacts supposed by mainman Morgan Buckley and his pal Ben Donohoe, a 12-track guess-again sprawl ranging from Arthur Russell-esque mood music to screwed Aphex jams.

Under the auspices of “Sworx”, an omniscient dialup modem, they parse coded waveforms in a discrete filing system, combing and recombining its data in a dozen buzzing post-techno chimeras and itchy electro jams. It’s instant classic Wah Wah Wino, freakishly playful and exerting odd sidespins on familiar styles and patterns with a ludic moxie that makes all their music so appealing.

The ‘Sworx’ system speaks its piece in a unique voice of detuned twangs and ululating electronic rhythms, shifting mercurial from what sounds like The Necks doing electro with a prepared piano on ‘OpportuniXt’, to a standout electro zinger with early AFXian vocaloids on ‘The System Works’, and Plone-esque key clatter on ‘dxmmy. pxtsy. rolodex’, thru a centrepiece calling to mind Oval’s most sublime on ‘breathwx (half_life)’. 

‘Western_intel [ frontier 2056 ]’ projects an unusually optimist vision of futurism, less techno dread, more cyber-pastoral, and the trip continues to wend from displaced, outernational folk in ‘Langley Prayer Room 9’, to a masterstroke of pitchbent club sauce in ‘sWORxism_noclocks_notimekept’ that tickles rarest pleasure centres with its piquant wrong-notes and gooey groove.

Collect them all!
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以虚构的拨号调制解调器系统“Sworx”为概念，将故障化电子节拍与超现实主义民谣碎片编织成十二首难以归类的曲目。创作者Morgan Buckley与Ben Donohoe在离散的数据档案中反复重组声音素材，呈现出从Arthur Russell式氛围情绪到扭曲的Aphex Twin式律动的宽阔光谱。作品游走于后工业电子与俏皮电音之间，既有类似The Necks用预置钢琴演奏电子乐的段落，也有早期AFX人声合成器点缀的亮眼曲目，甚至包含对Oval式极简美学的呼应。整张专辑在失谐拨弦、呜咽电子节奏与错音俱乐部律动中不断转向，展现出一种乐观的赛博田园未来感，而非常见的科技恐慌。其幽默感与对既有风格的歪斜处理，使熟悉的声音模式焕发出陌生的趣味。

items.body:
Pushing back against "Acid Nostalgia", Lawrence English dreams of a moonlit future on 'The Rest is My Ghost', bringing in assistance from a heap of collaborators, including members of The Necks, Swans, Mats Gustafsson, Rully Shabara and Lena Ito for a strong set that’s more curdled than harmonious, and all the better for it.

'The Rest is My Ghost' is more radical and political than anything we’ve heard from English in a while, more in line with 2014's charged 'Wilderness of Mirrors' and its brilliant follow-up 'Cruel Optimism’. Provoked by a conversation with Adam Curtis and driven by texts from Mark Fisher, JG Ballard, Katsuhiro Otomo, Franco Berardi, Kate Crawford and Alexie Yurchak and cultural architectural realities like the loss of Los Angeles' signature street lamps and Japan's Metabolists, English searches for a "political projection of nostalgia" that he can subsequently rupture. "Like acid poured onto a surface," he writes. "this use of nostalgia seeks to erode the complexity and texture of lived connection and longing, which has until recently guided contemplations of nostalgia."

He's talking about the difference between dreaming of your own past and being sold a neatly packaged pseudo-reality, its highs and lows smoothed over for easier consumption. To represent this concept musically, English moves away from dense distortions and instead collects up instrumental performances from a wide swathe of notable players including The Necks’ Chris Abrahams and Tony Buck, Madeleine Cocolas, Mats Gustafsson, Thor Harris, Heinz Riegler and Swans’ Norman Westberg among an all-star lineup. Perusing the personnel list and projecting your expectations on the material is part of the process and so English obscures everything purposefully, shrouding the instrumentation in reverb and gusts of hazed interference. If seeing names like pedal steel player Chuck Johnson gives you pause, that's the point. English engages in his own hauntological process, extracting the essence from the stems and imprinting it on his soundscapes. He's not eroding the material, but rather searching out the triggers that play on the imagination, inspiring futures that have never been more difficult to grasp.

And if it sounds dark, it's really not supposed to. Listen through the nocturnal hums and gentle, thrumming ambiance and you'll discover more than you bargained for - even a glimmer of hope. The result is a record that lands somewhere between classic Vangelis, Les Disques du Crépuscule's post-classical gear, Eno's fourth world experiments with John Hassell and Alan Lamb's influential sound art. In a world of drone and ambient musics that increasingly feel honed to numb the senses, this one tugs at something much deeper and more elemental.
items._genre: ambient / drone / experimental / electronic / fourth world
items._cn_summary: 劳伦斯·英格利希在新专辑中对抗“酸怀旧”思潮，以政治性视角重构记忆与未来的关系。受到亚当·柯蒂斯对话启发，并援引马克·费舍尔、J.G.巴拉德等文本，他邀请包括The Necks、Swans成员及松原幸夫等众多乐手参与，但刻意将器乐演奏淹没在混响与干扰气流中，使合作者的身份成为触发想象的符号而非风格标签。作品在夜间嗡鸣与轻柔震颤中展开，既延续了英格利希对声景质地的探索，又比以往更接近第四世界与后古典美学的交汇地带，同时保留了对黑暗现实的清醒凝视。专辑并非单纯的氛围铺陈，而是通过模糊化处理素材，让怀旧本身成为可被侵蚀和重新投射的媒介，最终在幽暗底色中透出微光。

items.body:
KAKUHAN / Sara Udon cellist Yuki Nakagawa takes a solemn yet dreamlike debut solo bow on the Unheard of Hope label - home to Mabe Fratti -  intently focussed on holistic examinations of his instrument, revealing its inner voices via various raw and processed strategies. RIYL Leila Bordreuil, Ecka Mordecai, Hildur Guðnadóttir, Okkyung Lee or Judith Hamann.

It's hard to explain just how eerily familiar Nakagawa's playing is, but you'll understand what we mean after hearing just a few moments of 'You Haze - I'. We've grown fully accustomed to the way Nakagawa handles the cello without even realizing it, absorbing his technique on records from KAKUHAN, his duo project with Koshihiro Hino, and Sara Udon alongside Naarm duo CS + Kreme. The way Nakagawa rests his bow between tones, picking up animated off-notes that make his sustained drones sound deep, dark and resonant, is genuinely personal, identifiable immediately. And although that aspect of his performance is front and center on his debut's opening track, it's the additional elements that tip us over the edge: the discreet, theremin-like wails that occupy a space just in the corner of the composition. 

After establishing his signature, Nakagawa veers away from his own convention sharply on 'CHU-MA', plucking the cello's strings and bending them as if they were attached to a koto. It's all remarkably stark at first, without much enhancement from Nakagawa's pedals and he slowly teases in different sounds that widen the instrument's range: woody creaks, knocks and growls that fill out its body and piercing overtones that go beyond the usual confines of the strings. Somehow, even using all these extended techniques, Nakagawa still manages to make music that's effortlessly enjoyable. It's bumpy, self-consciously experimental material, but not without roots - maybe best compared to Fred Frith's 'Guitar Solos' or Hans Reichel's 'The Death of the Rare Bird'.

There's even a prettiness to tracks like 'Upper and under the bridge' and 'You Haze - II' that betrays Nakagawa's resolve. But he's best when he's operating on the far fringe, turning his cello into a drum kit on the rickety, brilliant 'Grey test hits' or a vast resonator on the perplexingly huge 'Sange / Tsuki', an 8-minute xenharmonic spiral that sounds like an orchestra of fingerdrummed steel pans and a set of metal sheets being bowed in a concrete cavern. There's nothing else quite like it, we're sure of that.
items._cn_summary: 日本大提琴家中川由纪的首张个人专辑，以独奏形式展开对乐器整体性的深入检视。开篇曲以琴弓在音符间的停顿带出鲜活余音，使持续低音显得深沉而暗哑，角落还隐约漂浮着类似特雷门琴的呜咽声。随后他迅速偏离既有手法，像弹奏筝一样拨弦并弯折琴弦，加入木质吱呀、敲击、低吼与泛音等扩展技法，拓宽了琴体声响边界。部分曲目带有出乎意料的优美感，但最强烈的段落出现在边缘：将大提琴当作鼓组敲击，或在八分钟的微分音螺旋中制造出如同手指敲击钢鼓与金属板在混凝土洞穴中摩擦的庞大共鸣。整张专辑在个人化技法与大胆声响实验之间保持平衡，显示出对乐器潜能的独特理解。

items.body:
Thee most coveted collection of Coil demos surfaces on CD, opening a window onto the recording sessions for their pivotal 1991 release, ‘Love’s Secret Domain’. 

Originally collated on a demo tape for WaxTrax! records in 1989 under the working title ‘The Side Effects of Life’, these are the raw early iterations of tracks that would become ‘Love’s Secret Domain’, and arguably one of the ’90s definitive albums. Only a handful of the original cassette are known to exist, and have understandably become important artefacts in their own right, so it’s a massive buzz to finally, physically grasp the album in its entirety, here supplemented by material off the ‘Wrong Eye/Scope’ 7”.

Between the album’s two bookending versions of ‘Fidgit’, which later appeared on the ‘WaxTrax! Sampler #2’ tape in 1989, the album spools familiar yet rawer examples of Coil classics such as ‘Dark River’, ‘Teenage Lightening’ and ‘Love's Secret Domain’, each replete with haphazard fades, cuts and stereo bias, and often with lots of ferric noise. However none of that should put prospective listeners off, with results more faithful to the original than the weirdly pitched version found on YouTube and p2p sites.   

Ultimately it’s a proper find for Coil diehards, but anyone intrigued by the hidden reverse of what was going on in parallel to Rave, grunge and post rock in the phase shift between later ‘80s and early ‘90s, should fill their boots.
items._cn_summary: 这张作品收录了该乐队为一九九一年专辑《爱的秘密领域》录制的早期样带，原始素材来自一九八九年提交给唱片公司的试听带《生命的副作用》。与最终版相比，这些版本更粗糙，保留了大量磁带底噪、随意的淡入淡出、剪辑痕迹和左右声道偏移，呈现出创作过程中的未完成状态。此次实体发行还收录了同期七英寸单曲中的补充素材。乐评指出，这些录音比网上流传的变速版本更接近原始声音，是理解该组合在八十年代末至九十年代初与锐舞、垃圾摇滚、后摇滚并行发展的另一条脉络的重要材料。

items.body:
One of the most distinctive and legendary vocal/dub albums of all time, recorded in 1981 by the “dub dentist” Keith Hudson, ‘Playing It Cool & Playing It Right’ is now back in circulation for the first time in over 20 years, when it was first given overdue flowers via Basic Channel And Honest Jon’s ‘Basic Replay’ programme. It still burns with a rare energy, making it an untouchable, foundational text for the ages.

Keith Hudson (1946-1984) was one of dub reggae’s most distinctive innovators, renowned for a run of classic solo albums and productions for U-Roy, Big Youth, Ken Boothe and Horace Andy between 1972 and his untimely passing in 1984. However, Hudson's late period is where the real imperial juice can be found, a time that saw him move from Jamaican to London and New York studios, applying his unfathomable production style to a heavily americanised strain of vocal Soul. ‘Playing It Cool & Playing It Right’ is the pinnacle of that late period, an album that builds layer upon layer of alchemical brilliance.

Hudson’s combination of hooks and complex, highly unusual production is really unlike anything else from the period, or since, crooning in a soul mode made more haunting by a discreetly judicious application of tape FX, endlessly heavy subs, and mixing desk tricks deployed to delirious, almost psycho-acoustic effect.  The album was originally meant to feature one of Hudson's teenage sons to voice the dubs, but in the event the Love Joys, Wayne Jarrett, and inimitably Hudson himself featured at the microphone, with the dozen cuts co-produced by Wackies founder Lloyd ‘Bullwackie’ Barnes - the only collaboration between the two producers. It was originally issued on Hudson’s own label, Joint International, with subsequent pressings on Basic Replay in 2003, making it increasingly sought-after in the years since. 

Alongside reggae’s first concept album, ‘Flesh of My Skin, Blood of My Blood’, ‘Playing It Cool’ remains one the genre’s most important and unusual releases, picking up new disciples with every new wave of listeners taken aback by its stark, brooding blooze and brittle, spectral rendering.
items._cn_summary: 这张1981年的专辑是牙买加制作人基思·哈德森晚期代表作。他从牙买加移师伦敦与纽约录音室，将达布制作思维注入美式灵魂乐，人声与厚重低音、磁带效果、调音台技巧层层叠加，形成迷幻而幽暗的声响。专辑由瓦基斯厂牌创始人劳埃德·巴恩斯共同制作，是两人唯一合作；人声由拉夫乔伊、韦恩·贾勒特及哈德森本人担当。该作在达布与雷鬼历史中被视为开创性文本，其怪异的制作方式与幽暗气质对后世影响深远。

items.body:
Weirder, wider, knottier and more hypnotic than its predecessors, L'rain's fourth album closes out her opening act with a vivid firework display of canny cultural references, considered observations and, most crucially, heartbreakingly beautiful songs. It's dumbfounding material, the kind of omnivorous, masterful gear that just doesn't come around often enough - a future classic, to put it bluntly, FFO keiyaA, Mabe Fratti, Dawuna, Dijon or even Broadcast.

There's an aura of comprehensiveness that surrounds 'fata morgana'. Taja Cheek has fully broken in her influences and inspirations at this stage and works without hesitation, painting out her experiences of a broken world with a level of insight that's so rare it's almost unparalleled. We already know that Cheek is a forensic listener; 2024's 'I Killed Your Dog' was a chunky "anti-break-up" album that met sorrow head-on with psych rock, indie, classic R&B and haunted folk references, while its predecessor projected Cheek's ambition, embedding shoegaze and ambient influences into a widescreen collage of avant-garde expressions. It wasn't fusion, exactly, it was Cheek's real-world experience - both as an artist and a high-profile curator - inked on thick, deluxe stock in illuminated letters. And the cycle that she began in 2017 with her tape saturated debut comes to a close with 'fata morgana'.

'I Killed Your Dog' was well aware of its lineage, recorded and produced with a level of detail that immediately put it alongside '70s avant-rock and R&B classics, so 'fata morgana' scratches away another layer, making deeper, odder connections. Even the brief 'rumors of light' is anything but throwaway, casually introducing Cheek's voice through a hailstorm of looped interference that's broken up by disarming bouts of silence. This doesn't only slickly establish the record's experimental credentials, it echoes the eerie 'Transmission' tracks on DJ Shadow's 'Endtroducing'. "This is not a dream," a garbled voice memorably stated, and Cheek's utterances hint at the exact opposite, a choppy mess of backmasked syllables, coughs and hesitations that suggest we're being lowered into a surreal fantasy. Fairytale muted piano phrases appear in the distance and 'with time' materializes on the horizon, kinked by buzzing oscillations that blur time just slightly until Cheek's whisper-sung vocals sidestep into the candlelight. 

Already, it's Cheek's most enigmatic track, occupying the confounding spot between an acid-tweaked Laurel Canyon memory, a half-heard gospel standard and Wendy Carlos's iconic 'The Shining' score: beautiful, meaningful and effortlessly cinematic. And Cheek continues to paint outside the lines, concocting half-song 'blue' from tape-mangled brass loops and gunky drum improvisations that she scrapes into a seductive, hazed atmosphere underneath her reverberating chorals. It's tempting to reference shoegaze or dream pop; the end result is similar, texturally at least, but 'fata morgana' is comprised of hardier raw material: minerals crushed by hand from funk, spiritual jazz, reggae, blues and rock 'n roll. That's never more obvious than on the gorgeous 'july 5th', when smudged folk - mixed with screaming feedback and analog bleeps, of course - mutates into a jerky soundsystem banger in its final act, imagining what OutKast's 'B.O.B.' might sound like if Atlanta was swapped out for Kingston.

Then there's the brassy standout 'elmyra', an anthemic start-stop post-pop banger that's part 'Haha Sound'-era Broadcast and part Wire, distorted to a level that would terrify most green-gilled pretenders. All this, and we haven't even mentioned the album's dense, maximalist lead single 'Soulless Cycle', a track that begins with chattering, bit-crushed samples and double-time kicks and lunges towards its glittering, psychedelic wall of sound that stands as an apt metaphor for the melancholy cacophony of contemporary reality. Before the album's done, Cheek slides in a lysergic slow jam ('birthday') and a near-ambient darkjazz diversion ('church of no one'), reminding us that perseverance and resilience is still possible - preferable, in fact.

Seriously, it's one of those albums that reminds you why you started caring about music in the first place, a milestone that's both cognizant of its place in history and hyper aware of the current moment. So, so good.
items._genre: experimental / avant-garde / psychedelic / art pop / ambient / shoegaze
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是主创的第四张作品，也是她自二〇一七年开启的创作周期的收束。乐评形容其比前作更怪异、更宽广、更缠绕、更具催眠感，并强调其杂食性融合：迷幻摇滚、经典节奏布鲁斯、鬼魅民谣、自赏与氛围声响被拼贴成半成品式的歌谣结构。开篇曲以循环干扰、反向人声、咳嗽与沉默片段制造坠落感；随后一曲用振荡嗡鸣模糊时间，低语人声如烛光般切入；另一首则以磁带损伤的铜管循环和粘稠鼓点即兴铺底，再叠入混响合唱。乐评特别指出其拼接手法呼应经典采样拼贴作品，并带有温蒂·卡洛斯恐怖片配乐般的电影感。整张专辑在断裂与流畅之间保持平衡，既有前卫声响实验，也有清晰的旋律书写。

items.body:
Stefan Betke aka Pole’s hugely influential debut LP of frayed dub experiments resurfaces for a 20th anniversary reissue, taking us back to smoked out nights at the turn of the century and some of the finest post basic-channel dub echoes ever released. Essential listening if you’re into anything from Rhythm & Sound to Vainqueur, Jon Hassell to Jackie Mittoo.

As legend goes, Pole took his name from a malfunctioning Waldorf 4-Pole filter which produced hisses and pops which weren’t really controllable or predictable, much like a living organism. Betke realised the potential and came to alchemically morph and render them with judicious FX dubbing into a groundbreaking sort of minimalist electro-dub that sounds exceedingly good with a spliff and glass of booze. Working somewhere between the variants of abstract techno on Chain Reaction and Mille Plateaux’s cutting edge minimalist strains, Pole’s first trio of albums inarguably helped lay the foundations for dub techno as it’s come to be known and are held in the highest regard by practically everyone who owns them. 

The Pole aesthetic is patently laid out in ‘1’, where his organic clicks ’n pops come out to play accompanied by lilting organ and jazzy bass channelling Jackie Mittoo via Jon Hassell and Rhythm & Sound into a uniquely, gauzy, gaseous state.  So strong was the impact of the album on the late ‘90s underground, they even generated a “pastiche” that was unwittingly issued (and subsequently deleted) by Fat Cat on their split series, but was purportedly made by V/Vm in a snidey but frankly hilarious prank, albeit one that demonstrates just how ubiquitous and influential Betke’s sound was at the time. More than that, it’s fair to say the 20 year cycle hasn’t rinsed out the appeal of this triptych one bit; it remains one of electronic music’s most enigmatic and strangely moving, tactile bodies of work.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Stefan Betke以Pole为名发表的处女作，源自一台故障的Waldorf 4-Pole滤波器所产生的不稳定嘶嘶声与爆音。他将这些如同有机体般难以预测的杂音，通过延迟与效果处理，转化为一种极简电子与dub深度融合的声响。作品中贯穿的风琴与爵士贝斯线条，在细碎颗粒与烟雾般的空间感中交织，呈现出介于Chain Reaction抽象科技舞曲与Mille Plateaux极简主义之间的独特气质。专辑对90年代末地下电子场景影响深远，甚至引发了恶搞式的模仿发行，足见其声音语汇的渗透力。时隔二十年，这张唱片依然保持着实验性与触感上的新鲜度，是理解dub techno脉络不可绕过的作品。

items.body:
Reissue of the debut by A.G. Cook & Danny L Harle’s earliest duo, Dux Content, initially dispensed on Gamsonite, a predecessor of P.C. Music, and teasing out strands of makina, electro-house, bardcore and trap with combo’s of ludic, recombinant suss & sharp sound design that became their calling card.

Scrolling back to what now feels like a distant world - the up-for-grabs edges of early 2010s - ‘Lifestyle’ maps out formative aspects of the two producers, still relatively fresh from music studies at Goldsmiths, and making their mark in a burgeoning “internet music” scene. Of course they’re both now chart-topping songwriters/producers with credits for Charli xcx, Dua Lipa, Oklou, et al, but here they’re positively bubbling over with wild, yet disciplined, fusions of upfront hard dance with jazz, contemporary classical and pop that, with the benefit of hindsight, place them in a contemporaneous cultural slipstream with likes of Cracksmurf/T C F or James Ferraro, and soon-to-be spar, SOPHIE.

‘Lifestyle’ is the sound of two minds scything thru cultures and sounds they grew up with - Harle coming from a family background spanning his Geordie dad, John Harle’s BBC scores and early taste for makina’s stacked melodies - and bonding over a shared love of Captain Beefheart, Archie Sheep, and Tim & Eric, all evident in their grasp of shiny, commercial hooks and complex rhythm wrapped up with daft grin and wink. Shake a wand anywhere and you’ll hit a mad one, from the crazed midi piano house of ‘Voice of an Angel’, thru the jazz-fink of ‘City Break’ and ‘Hero Next Door’, free wheeling jazz trance of ‘Heart of Death’ and pitch bent panpipes of ‘Business Class’.
items._genre: experimental electronic / makina / electro-house / jazz fusion / trap
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是A.G. Cook与Danny L Harle早期组合Dux Content的首张作品再版，融合了makina、electro-house、trap、爵士与当代古典等元素。两人在Goldsmiths求学后，以游戏般的重组手法和锐利的声音设计，将硬核舞曲与爵士、古典、流行拼贴在一起，展现出早期互联网音乐场景的鲜活能量。乐评指出其风格与Cracksmurf、James Ferraro及SOPHIE等处于同一文化脉络，并体现出对Captain Beefheart、Archie Sheep和Tim & Eric的趣味。曲目如《Voice of an Angel》的疯狂MIDI钢琴浩室、《City Break》与《Hero Next Door》的爵士放克、《Heart of Death》的自由爵士恍惚感，以及《Business Class》的变调排笛，均展示了两人在商业感与复杂节奏之间的独特平衡。

items.body:
Recorded live in Brooklyn, 'Somewhere in the Wind' is Loren Connors & David Grubbs’ third album and their first as a guitar duo, showcasing their free-er, noiser side with two extended, ecstatic jams. 

Thankfully, we didn't have to wait another two decades to hear Grubbs and Connors collide again. Their first album, 'Arborvitae', appeared way back in 2003, not long after the duo had first met when Connors shared a bill with Gastr del Sol. But it wasn't until 2024 that they rekindled that magic, shaking things up a little and swapping roles on keys and guitar, with Connors even moonlighting on drums. 'Somewhere in the Wind' might be the perfect companion to that record, recorded last year at Blank Forms, it's their first session featuring both players on electric guitar and it's a joy to engage with on every level. Both distinctive players carry an unmistakable signature style, complementing each other by leaning into the noise and freedom of their collaboration in a way we hadn't witnessed until now. 

If their first two records dug into crepuscular space, the domain of Roy Montgomery and Harold Budd, this one takes its cues from the physicality of their instruments and the knowledge they've acquired along the way. You feel as if you're practically in the room with them as Connors's blurry post-blues recitals casually interact with Grubbs' obsessively tuned intonations. On the first side, we walk into what might as well be a prayer, each note played in reverence to something or someone. But as the piece accumulates weight, so too do the notes, lovingly distorted and pushed off track until all that's left is raw emotion. On the flip, the duo sound even more possessed, kicking up the energy so the notes bounce around the very edges of the recording space. It's a document of two players who don't have anything left to prove.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是两位音乐家继2003年合作后的再次碰撞，也是他们首次以双电吉他二重奏形式进行录音。两首长篇即兴作品展现了更自由、更噪音的一面，康纳斯模糊的后蓝调乐句与格拉布斯高度调校的音响相互交织。第一面如同祈祷，每个音符都带有仪式感，随着声音累积逐渐失真，最终化为纯粹的情感；第二面能量更为充沛，音符在录音空间边缘弹跳。整张专辑记录了两位演奏者之间无需证明的默契，强调乐器的物理性与长期积累的经验，让听者仿佛置身现场。

items.body:
Anyone obsessed with those two incredible ‘Begena Songs…’ comps on Death Is Not The End will be properly enchanted by this more expansive - yet still intimate - suite of snapshots from Ethiopia, 1971, spanning the unique, twanging harp sound thru to Amharic poetry, chants, and spellbinding flute dances...

One that catches the breath with seldom felt sensations, ‘Ethiopian Musics 1971’ patently owes as much to the incredible performers as their faithful representation in Ragnar Johnson & Ralph Harrisson’s recordings. All secreted to tape on a Uher Report L stereo reel-to-reel recorder, they epitomise an era of ethnomusicological preservation, when the likes of labels such as Lyrichord and  Folkways were already decades deep “in the field”, documenting long-held traditions practically untouched by an encroaching, western modernity. And perhaps most crucially, the recordings beautifully render the acoustic settings and vivid vibes with an immersive quality in stark opposition to the era of dry, so-called audiophile studio recordings of ethnic musics to come - all the better for immersing in this wonderfully unfamiliar world.

The abundance of singular tones and strong, rare feels they produce is quite staggering to our northern english ears, and we reckon also for anyone else, for that matter. Opening to a joyful couplet of a bluesy ’Song about the beauty of women’, and the almost shanty-like swing and hard rhythm of ’Tej Beit Song’, the set reels to distinctive pieces of Ethiopian Christian song set to begena, or ‘Harp of David’, buzz, and a landscape-scale, 13 minute ‘Love Song (Mary Armede)’. A gripping ‘Drum Song (Jigsaw)’ will be mana to rhythm fiends, and a number of standout flute pieces reprise the frisson of our first encounter with this discipline on Sublime Freq’s ‘Staring into the Sun - Ethiopian Tribal Music’ set of 2012, most potently on the pluming twin pipes of the ‘Fila Flute Dance’ parts, whilst the pentatonic craar (6-stringed lyre) parts surely strike nerves for lovers of the rawest blues, and hail the liberated legacy of Mary Armede, a folk singer-fashion designer of Azmari heritage who surely warrants further investigation. 

No doubt this is one of the most striking archival discoveries of 2026, acutely advised to anyone enchanted with music from this corner of the world from Éthiopiques to begena harp, thru to Ragnar Johnson’s other arenas of research for Ideologic Organ in Yemen or Papua New Guinea. Dive in without delay.
items._genre: ethiopian traditional / field recording / folk / world music
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录了1971年在埃塞俄比亚录制的民间音乐，由Ragnar Johnson与Ralph Harrisson使用Uher Report L便携录音机完成。内容涵盖贝格纳竖琴、阿姆哈拉诗歌、基督教圣歌、笛舞及六弦里拉琴等表演，呈现了当地多样的音乐传统。录音保留了现场声学环境与演奏氛围，具有直接而沉浸的质感，与后来流行的干涩录音室民族音乐录音形成对比。乐评特别提到Mary Armede的13分钟爱情歌曲以及多首笛舞曲目，强调其独特的音色与节奏。这批录音被视为重要的档案发现，对关注埃塞俄比亚音乐传统及民族音乐学录音的听众具有参考价值。

items.body:
Colin Stetson’s breakthrough album of gripping bass sax innovations still buzzes like few others.

In 2007 ‘New History Warfare Vol.1’ asserted Stetson as an indomitable player of wind instruments, here letting off on Alto, Baritone and Bass Saxophones, plus Clarinet, in a deftly muscular display of his skills which had previously been employed on record and in live tours for Arcade Fire, Tom Waits, Bon Iver, LCD Soundsystem and whoever the heck else needed a set of lungs as good as a blacksmith’s bellows.

While perhaps best known for wielding a massive Bass Saxophone that's responsible for some of the wildest sounds on this album, Stetson proves to be a sensitive beast capable of articulating the instrument’s full range tonal in his own voice, which variously comes out resembling a purring big cat and the dying wildebeest it just stalked, attacked and slaughtered in ‘Time Is Advancing With Fitful Irregularity’, while he uses the same broad tone to describe natural scenes as textured with soil and moisture and wind as an Anne Guthrie piece in ‘As a Bird or Branch’, while ‘Nobu Take’ sounds like a manic 8-bit computer game soundtrack and ’Tiger Tiger Crane’ adds a tight percussive workout for good measure, but trust its all acoustic, instrumental, hands-on, somehow not processed. 

Still a stonking good record, this, ripe for re/discovery.

items.body: In July, Europe was grappling with extremely high temperatures and, as a result, thunderstorms due to the heat dome over the continent. I live on the top floor of an apartment building and therefore had a particularly privileged view of these natural spectacles. On one occasion, I could see such a storm approaching - a dark wall rapidly pushing toward the city - though it was obvious that the weather front would only graze the city. The gusts of wind were fierce, trees bent under the force of nature, thunder roared, and lightning lit up the sky. But why am I telling you this? Because it fits perfectly with “Equilibrum”, the first track on the new album by the international trio Okuda Müller Hall - Rieko Okuda (Japan; piano), Matthias Müller (Germany, trombone), and Samuel Hall (Australia, drums) - perfectly. At first, the drums just tingle softly; Hall rubs the toms and strokes the cymbals, while Müller delivers an unsettling drone that shifts only slightly. Sometimes it grows louder, then fades again; it literally fluctuates. Then the piano slowly enters the picture, with Okuda attacking the interior of the instrument. Almost imperceptibly, everything grows louder, darker, and more menacing. The thunderstorm is now over you, but only a few heavy drops are falling, symbolized by isolated piano notes. Even though you know you’ll get off lightly, a hauntingly beautiful, fascinating feeling lingers. “Six Lights,” the third and longest track on the album, continues this form of improvisation in a similar vein. Müller, however, forgoes the drone, opting instead for deliberate, sustained notes over which Okuda showers bright piano sprinkles, while Hall works his magic on the dark drums and simultaneously manipulates extended materials. Müller then takes a two-and-a-half-minute break, and when he rejoins the piece, it actually sounds like contemporary European free jazz or like - say - a trippy ECM recording. In general, ³√ (“Cube Root”) combines wide-ranging developments with a finely balanced structure, it’s a perfect showcase of Berlin’s Echtzeitmusik scene, the trio’s music flows organically into a distinct sonic language - multi-layered, crystal clear, a combination of density and openness. The liner notes mention that an “acoustic space of great depth and fluidity unfolds, within which a steady pull develops, drawing the listener ever deeper into this flowing, ever-changing soundscape“. My favorite track on the album, though, is the last one, “Sputnik.” The thunder and lightning of the opener are gone; what remains is the wind - rough, wild, hissing around the corners and producing strange sounds. Rieko Okuda creates a powerful soundscape against which Müller and Hall enjoy a great deal of freedom, and which ultimately proves what they are - in a musical sense: a force of nature. The album ends with a few subtle dabs of piano. Fascinating and stunningly beautiful. ³√ is available as a download. You can listen to the cording here: ³√ by Okuda Müller Hall Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Label: Pi Recordings, 2026 Personnel - Henry Threadgill: alto saxophone, flute, bass flute; Liberty Ellman: acoustic guitar; Jose Davila: tuba, trombone; Christopher Hoffmann: cello; Elliott Humberto Kavee: drums. I dig Henry Threadgill’s type of sound, how he orchestrates modern classical, progressive chamber jazz, and avant-garde opaqueness using layers that unfold with meticulously planned coherence and originality. Threadgill’s prominent presence on the contemporary avant-garde landscape has a strong association with Zooid, a tight quintet that has never felt so loose as in Cut You Where You Was . Threadgill is not heading into a new direction here, but the album has plenty to discover and enjoy. On “ Fluoroscope ”, we notice intervallic leaps within a highly contrapuntal environment, which is so characteristic of the saxophonist’s style. With a tight focus on arrangement and composition, the piece also counts on mystifying solos by Threadgill, who uncorks atypical melodies, and guitarist Liberty Ellman, whose acoustic patterns sound just right over the textural oddities generated by cellist Christopher Hoffman, tubist José Davila, and drummer Elliott Humberto Kavee. The three-movement chamber piece “ Bingo ” explores a variety of exquisite feels and moods: “ Bingo Part 1 ” sets elated flute flights against tuba wails, low-key guitar specifications, and somber cello; “ Bingo Part 2 ” features Ellman’s bluesy slide technique as flute and trombone contribute to the exotic, picturesque landscape; and “ Bingo Part 3 ” thrives on motivic alto sax and enthralled mallet drumming. “ Red Admiral Red Moon Rising ” is the album’s centerpiece, clocking in at more than 12 minutes. What begins as a mournful dirge with plenty of delightful detail quickly evolves into a captivating, quirky groove that has its own imaginative way of swinging. Only Threadgill can come up with these rhythmic jaw-droppers, and his dissonant solo here resonates within that narrative thrust. His ability to go against structural norms and jazz conventions is also mirrored on “ Off And On What Happened ”, where the inventive, unaccompanied Kavee shines. Counterpoint and fragmented cadences are injected before the skillful drummer finishes what he had started. “ Lightnin’ ” is another miniature gem, with sax and guitar declaring curious lines in unison and a deliciously offbeat groove underpinning Ellman’s clear yet nonconformist statement. Passion and openness are present throughout the album, and the final result is simultaneously haunting and bewitching. Favorite Tracks: 04 - Bingo Part 3 ► 05 - Red Admiral Red Moon Rising ► 07 - Off And On What Happened ► 08 - Lignin’

items.body:
“The thing about playing the tuba in an orchestra is that you don’t have to play that much,” admitted composer Matthew Wright, who grew up playing the tuba in orchestras and funk bands, “but it’s the best seat in the house. You hear music back to front. The percussion and the brass are loud, so you hear all their detail, and the strings are this kind of ethereal thing that’s off in the distance.”

For the Kent-based Wright, who also improvises using turntables, samplers, and processers – most impactfully with Trance Map, his partnership with Evan Parker – this early realization nurtured a sensibility leading to the creation of immersive works that mix composition, improvisation, and technology. Cracked Glaze (False Walls) is a case in point, as it utilizes notated material – “dot music” is his good-humored term – improvisation, and Wright’s real-time sampling and processing immediately fed into surround sound, all of which he remixed for the CD.

Wright’s collaborators on Cracked Glaze represent various facets of his work. Ensemble Klang, an ensemble of mostly Dutch new music virtuosi, was an early champion of Wright’s compositions. Spheric Totemic is a Wright-instigated, flexibly configured improvising group with, on this occasion, Mandhira de Saram, Alexander Hawkins, Neil Charles and Stephen Davis. Sofia Jernberg, whose Musho with Hawkins was one of the brighter lights of 2024, is new to Wright’s constellation.

Historically, the conventional wisdom among exponents of freely improvised music is that the larger the group, the more apt the music will be muddied. It is a yardstick that is also prevalent among practitioners of contemporary composition. Individuality – of the improviser, of the composer – is more difficult to assert in or through a crowd. Although there are more than a dozen musicians heard on Cracked Glaze, there is no nebulous sprawl or complexity for complexity’s sake. Abstraction is tethered to figuration, the spine of the piece being a descending line that repeatedly submerges and reemerges, giving the interactions of voices clear relationships.

“In a lot of my written work for ensembles there is a central concern that tends to last a long period of time, an idea that will give the piece structure. I’m really interested in music being a kind of terrain that you can hear through and around, so that when you are listening, you are experiencing a kind of ‘visual’ situation. I guess this goes back to my work with vinyl records, because records make music a physical surface, where you can place the needle anywhere in the terrain of the music.

“In the improvised work, I don’t want to be the guy that says to improvisers, ‘this is how it goes.’ Improvisation, in a free context, is about distributed leadership. It’s about this beautiful situation of people saying, ‘the music could go here’ or ‘I hear the future of this music in what you’re playing,’ and the kind of listening that leads to those sorts of situations.

“Having the opportunity to work with a group that is mainly readers – Ensemble Klang – and a group that is mainly improvisers – Spheric Totemic – and Sofia Jernberg, gave me the opportunity to do something I haven’t done much of in my music, to have a spine that is unfurling but is always there. It doesn’t necessarily always have to be the main focus of the piece, but it will always be there. It will structure time in a certain way; improvisers can do whatever they want to do, and the music will be as much about them as it is the spine. I was really interested in having a sort of ‘object’ in the space of the improvisation. It’s almost like in the visual art world, where you have people moving around in a gallery but there’s a sculpture there. It’s in the room with you.”

Another virtue of Cracked Glaze is that it is the type of work that initially seems to come out of nowhere. It smacks of singularity. However, Wright’s backstory reveals that he did not come out of nowhere, as he has a pedigree linking him to England’s most consequential institutional incubator of experimental music, as well as its most venerable, living exponent of improvised music. Both associations largely account for how Wright’s disparate interests – several of which were common among Gen Xers in their formative years but were delayed in being assimilated into experimental music – were shaped into a mature aesthetic, and yielded in Cracked Glaze an arguably definitive statement.

“My experience, first of all, was writing music and playing in brass bands and funk bands and small improvising groups with friends,” Wright recently explained. “But I also liked writing chamber music for people who would take it away and play it somewhere else. I might not even be there for the performance. This background took me to study at the University of Huddersfield with the Professor who set up the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival, Richard Steinitz. I was very lucky. It was kind of random. He was my composition teacher. So, I was very lucky to have experiences like knocking on the door for a composition lesson and Richard Steinitz saying, ‘Ah, Matt, I can’t possibly teach you right now, but meet Karlheinz,’ and the door opens and there’s this world-famous composer from another generation that I had read about, but never dreamed I would meet.

“Contemporary classical music was a big part of my education, but I DJed as a kid. I was really interested at that point in the ‘80s and ‘90s when software, sampling, and DJ technology, was becoming affordable. It started showing up in people’s homes. Contemporary classical music and DJ culture were colliding in my mind when I was a kid. The only kind of formal education I could get was a classical education, along with some jazz theory, but it was largely based on dot music, written music. Then there was this other (non-written) side, like DJ culture and all of the great heritage of Black music that DJ culture is part of, and that was a kind of informal education I studied for myself.

“When I was a real little kid – like 12 or 13 – I made a lot of bedroom productions with a basic computer and turntable setup, really focused on instrumental hip-hop. I started to scratch around then, just watching how it was done on TV. My main inspirations were DJ Premier of Gangstarr, Terminator X of Public Enemy, and Maseo of De La Soul. When I was around 18 or 19, as a student, I DJed for a few parties, playing mainly funk, hip hop, and drum ‘n' bass. Around the same time – 1996-98 – I was in a few pop/funk bands that needed a DJ, so I did a few things with beat juggling and matching the pitch of the horns with turntable scratches, etc.

“In 1999 I DJed for a social event at the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival and I decided to just play fragments of music that I loved at the time: The Jazz Warriors, Louis Andriessen, Loose Tubes, Squarepusher, Björk. On the basis of that weird mix, I got the call to DJ at Abbey Road for the launch of a music charity, the PRS Foundation, in 2000. That was both a social event and included some (not entirely successful!) experimental scratching. When I moved to Holland to study with composer Louis Andriessen in 2002, I joined a trio with laptop artist Tom Tlalim and saxophonist Keir Neuringer – now of Irreversible Entanglements – and we played a few house parties and small gigs with our own mix of free improv and beat-based electronica. That same year the Huddersfield Festival commissioned ‘Presents from an Edited Then’ which was a 70-minute piece for The Apollo Saxophone Quartet and me DJing, designed for a club venue, again a mix of ‘social’ and ‘experimental’. That’s when I got interested in the worlds of contemporary classical music and DJ culture colliding.”

One of the first projects Wright embarked on was to compose for turntables and to teach classically-trained percussionists how to use them, integrating John Cage’s early work for percussion with the innovations of Christian Marclay and Otomo Yoshihide. “In a piece called Contact Theatre I had literally written out all of the material for notation-reading percussionists”, Wright said of the work. “If you look at a musical stave with the four spaces between the lines, I used those spaces to represent the four spaces on a vinyl record. The space that would be a F in the treble stave, that’s the space on the outer edge of the record, before any musical material appears on the vinyl record. All of the musical material on the record is included in the second space, and then the space at the center of the record was the third space, and then the label itself in the fourth space. You can prepare those spaces, put stickers on them. I would literally write percussion rhythms and they could produce those rhythms by dropping the needle on the record and get a ricochet effect or specify a section of the record I want to be played, say a saxophone solo three minutes into the record. I developed these ‘half-contact’ techniques where the needle sticks like a locked groove, and I taught the basics of hip hop scratching to percussionists, even though the music didn’t sound anything like hip hop.”

Wright then began to assess the proportions of and the relationships between the elements of his aesthetic and how to integrate them in his work. “Cracked Glaze is a collision of all of the above. I have been doing ensemble work and turntable work and installation work, but a lot of my focus is on the work with Evan in mixing and even post-production of the Trance Map material. Post-production is really part of the process, and Evan is very interested in exploring all that. Although Cracked Glaze doesn’t involve Evan, it brings to equal terms all of the sources I work with. There’s some notation written for Ensemble Klang with holes in that notation, space for the improvisation group of Spheric Totemic and Sofia Jernberg. They have start and stop times for the improvising, and they also sometimes have cues for some notation. I’m also mixing them live on stage, taking samples and remixing them and using the turntable as well. Then I take all that material and work on it a little in the studio, not to radically change the piece but to bring out some of the elements that you would hear live but not in a stereo recording. The piece brings together notation, improvisation, and technology, but not as separate forms. They all intersect. That’s where they all join on the map.”

In a roundabout way, the title of the piece speaks to the processes of its creation. It refers to the glazes used in high-fire ceramics that are formulated to crack on temperature; even though they are applied in an even manner, the cracking results in a surface that can be likened to a mosaic assembled with random tiles, with dark, hair-thin spaces between them. Though the results are subject to a unique firing, the experienced artist knows how to promote cracking that is pleasing and avoid cracking that ruins the piece.

“It may be interesting to talk about how jazz standards have worked in the past,” Wright responded to the idea of controlled cracking, and chuckling at the notion that he controlled the gas valve. “An excellent standard is one that can be played in its entirety and feel integrated and beautiful, but it is also a catalyst. It offers itself up to be cracked, to be turned into something new. In some ways, the use of notation to suggest a response is fascinating to me. On a technical level, there are definitely moments where I say to the improvisers, ‘at a certain point you will hear a line and at that point, that pitch, that’s your moment; if you’re improvising, the natural ebb and flow of the group will go to you’. But I don’t say ‘you should crack it’ to them; I say ‘it’s yours’.

“And there’s a third element there, the equivalent of the heat – the processing and the spatialization. I’m taking the feed of everybody, the notated music and the improvised music is coming to my setup, and I’m able to remix it and sample it. I’m an agent in the cracking, too. Whether it is notated or not is not the point, because it’s all going through the same system and being splintered into surround sound. That’s the third element, the sound design is a catalytic element.”

Wright pointed to a poster in his studio of a still influential Japanese textile exhibition he attended in his early 20s. “What I loved about that,” he said, “was that the dynamic shapes of these textiles are very rigid, spatially, but the textiles themselves have all sorts of holes in them. They are almost like fishing nets. I tried to create something similar by creating a structure that’s flexible but has holes in it. If we play this piece again, the melody line and the structure is going to be exactly the same every time and the improvising and the specialization will be different every time. That’s a long-winded way of saying I tried not to over notate.”

Wright acknowledged that post-production, particularly when the work was created in a surround sound environment and is remixed for stereo, creates a distinct experience of the work, and perhaps represents a new iteration of the pursuit of perfection in the studio, exemplified by Glenn Gould. “My pieces are concepts that have a sort of quantum existence,” Wright maintained. “What I mean is that if we are going to present the piece live, then there are circumstances that will be dynamic for the audience in the live space that may not be so dynamic when hearing it at home. In the live space, I’m dealing with surround sound. There are a whole lot of options to try to present that sort of experience in the stereo format. When it comes to making a CD or something online that people will listen to, I consider the domestic setting. I also consider that many people listen to music on the go, with headphones or their phone. You may be walking down the Avenue of the Americas and everything around you is changing, but there’s one consistent thread in the music.

“You have to consider the multiple ways that people listen now. I do hope that people will sit at home to listen to it. In that situation, it’s much closer to reading a book because it’s a solitary experience. You’re sitting with it for 40 or 50 minutes. Wearing headphones creates an interior experience. I really treasure those kinds of listeners and it’s a real privilege when someone spends that time with something that I’ve made with my musical friends.

“In the history of improvised music there have been many vehement statements about the relationship between free improvised music and recording. I totally get that, but I suppose that the question we now have to consider is what happens when you improvise with a recording. We don’t want the karaoke thing! How does the recording come back into the improvised music experience in as fluid a way you would have with another musician with an instrument? An instrument is obviously a technology of its own and the recording is the result of the technology. We need to make sure the technology is as flexible as any other instrument. The other thing I’m really fascinated by in the history of free creative music is the evolution of incorporating electronics. It’s really interesting for me when an electro-acoustic improvised situation might suggest that the music is not happening in the present tense, but in the past or the future.

“The thing I’m really interested in is those previously separated camps of notation, improvisation, and technology becoming one and the same, where there is an equaling out of the three. You’re not relying on one form of expression. And this seems to be causing a real revitalization of the scene, where people are mastering their separate disciplines and are also negotiating with each other. I think there’s more opportunity for creative music because of the dialogue between notation, improvisation, and technology. Looking for the connections between them is the main creative impetus. It’s not paper; it’s not technology; it’s not adherence to one way of making music. It’s about thinking about the connections between the people you’re working with. Saying ‘all of the above’ may be too easy an answer, but it does ascribe equal value to notation, improvisation and technology. These are all zones on the map and they all overlap each other, so the paths between those zones are what I’m interested in.”

***

Wright’s projects frequently overlap, the post production of one coinciding with the development of another. With summer approaching, Wright was mixing a duo session with Pat Thomas that has the flavor of This is Trickster; a Spheric Totemic album, and a Trance Map + recording on which Parker and him are joined by harpist Milana Zaric and Richard Barrett.

The presence of Barrett is particularly intriguing, as he pioneered improvised electronic music beginning in the 1990s – largely through FURT, his partnership with Paul Obermayer – laying groundwork for Wright and others. Additionally, Barrett’s compositions are renowned for testing – and often surpassing – the presumed physical limits of instrumentalists.

Barrett and Wright are part of a trajectory of composers foregrounding technology in their work. An earlier dot on the line, one that is essential but not obvious, is Conlon Nancarrow. The expatriate composer is the inspiration for Wright’s next major work, “Passing Nancarrow.” Wright’s latest project with the Belgian ensemble BL!NDMAN (the exclamation point is intentional) also has Hawkins in a key role. The piece debuts next year, marking 30 years since Nancarrow died.

“The idea of the piece is based around Nancarrow being obsessed with Art Tatum’s playing,” Wright explained. “He sampled Tatum in the form of piano rolls, using technology from a hundred years ago. What we will do is, while Alex improvises in real time, his notes are captured and this will trigger all sorts of reactions from the group. In a way, we turn Alex’s music into a piano roll.”

Wright was partly inspired by the writer and documentary film director Helen Borton’s comment that jazz and blues collide like a “hurricane” in Nancarrow’s music. Replace “hurricane” with “Nancarrow” and you get the gist of Wright’s conceptualization for the recording he is currently mixing – “four hurricanes of all kinds of crazy sounds.” Wright also considered the music of Squarepusher, Aphex Twin, and other exponents of electronic dance music, that influenced him when Nancarrow died in 1997, leading him to include “strange, intelligent dance music in the piece.”

However, the nexus of Nancarrow, Barrett, and Wright, is the consideration of the limits of music humans can create in real time, and how to get to the edge of those limits, if not extend them.

“Nancarrow reached for impossible, post-human music. But in my current work, I don’t have an artistic interest in post-human AI. I’ve heard a lot of AI-generated music and read a lot of AI research, and the thing I’m already bored by is that AI can do almost anything. Like a musician that can play everything and just won’t stop playing to give space for others, AI doing anything and everything is boring to me when you don’t hear inspired choices and you don’t hear the human labor or the human need for considered space in the music. But, I’m open minded. I just haven’t heard anything that inspires me yet. Back to the human level, in Alex’s piano playing, there is that reaching beyond what is supposedly humanly possible, to reach a new vista for what is possible.

“You can say that, for his times, Nancarrow was making a post-human kind of music, but we should remember that he sat there, punching holes. So, I don’t hear a sort of pre-AI in his music, a piano that can do anything, but the blood and the hours of Nancarrow sitting maybe six months to create an explosive two minutes. I want to know how humans feel when they hear music and when they make music. If that is aided by technology, the idea is that the technology helps musical thinking like an instrument helps musical thinking. My interest in technology is the same as Alex’s interest in the piano, there’s a tradition of human tool use there that in a sense heightens the human listening experience if done successfully.

“Another thing I like about Nancarrow was that he was true to his beliefs, which is why he left the US for Mexico City, which resulted in him working in relative isolation. He just got on with it. A few people had experimented with the player piano before, but he made it his own. I appreciate that you can hear the edges in music and you’re OK with not being able to know everything beyond that edge. I guess the difference between the scene we have now and Nancarrow’s situation is that we can go to the edge together in a collaborative spirit.”
