items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: Omar Sosa在意大利Fazioli钢琴音乐厅进行了一次两小时的无脚本独奏即兴，后期混音中加入人声片段、打击乐、循环、田野录音与拾得声音，构成这张充满冥想与灵性色彩的专辑。受Monk影响，他坚持每次演奏都不同，以第一遍录音为灵魂的自然发声，拒绝风格标签，融合古巴音乐根源、爵士自由即兴与当代实验声响。疫情与婚姻变故的背景赋予作品沉思气质，而空旷音乐厅的混响与钢琴内部拨弦、抚弦等技法则营造出深邃的空间感。Sosa强调音乐应扎根传统并走向进化，以低频泛音连接更本能的感知层面，使专辑既私人又具普遍性。其创作方式与声音处理展现了高度的自发性和不可复制性，适合关注即兴、世界音乐与声音实验的听众。

items.body: With first quarter of 21st century, Iranian sound artist Pé continues a trajectory that began with gold bars made in dubai (2025) and gathered momentum on 40.8 tonnes of freedom (2025), moving away from the metaphysical concerns of earlier releases towards an engagement with what he describes as “shrugged off crimes against humanity.” However, the shift is not as abrupt as it first appears. If albums such as æzæl: eternity of nonexistence (2025), æbæd: through imagining eternity (2024), and æm: representations of nonexistence (2024) used abstract synthesiser improvisations to examine nonexistence and cosmological time, the recent works retain the same compositional discipline while redirecting it towards contemporary history. For Pé, this is not a rupture but an evolution: an attempt to extend philosophical enquiry through what he calls a “transdisciplinary approach.” That continuity is immediately apparent in the music itself. The four compositions remain resolutely abstract, built from slowly evolving drones, unstable resonances, distortion and spectral interference rather than melody or rhythm. Despite titles such as “82,448 palestinians,” “conservatively confirmed death toll,” and “courtesy of state of israel,” there are no documentary recordings, no explicit musical illustrations of violence, and no attempt to dictate an emotional response. Instead, the gulf between the factual precision of the titles and the ambiguity of the sound becomes the album’s central compositional device. As Pé suggests, that space is deliberately left for the listener to confront through their own cultural, political and personal position. Compared to 40.8 tonnes of freedom (2025), first quarter of 21st century feels noticeably tighter and more compressed. The earlier EP allowed individual spectral layers greater autonomy, often opening vast acoustic spaces in which metallic resonances, drones and noise could coexist with remarkable transparency. Here the pressure rarely lifts. Each piece explores a different manifestation of instability: the slowly mutating density of the title track, the relentless fragmentation of “82,448 palestinians,” the devastating restraint of “conservatively confirmed death toll,” and the architectural synthesis of “courtesy of state of israel.” Throughout, Pé continues to compose almost exclusively through the redistribution of spectral energy, microscopic timbral shifts and long-form transformations, demonstrating an exceptional command of electroacoustic form. The accompanying Bandcamp warning — “Listener discretion advised. Extreme frequencies low and high moderate volume suggested to avoid possible damages, please be cautious psychoacoustic effects intended” — proves more than justified. Pé’s music has always been deeply concerned with the physical experience of listening, and the sub-bass pressure, abrasive upper frequencies and carefully controlled beating phenomena are integral to the compositions. Those self-imposed limitations, including the recurring use of the ARP Odyssey and minimal post-production, have become a deliberately restricted vocabulary through which different conceptual territories can be explored. Few contemporary electroacoustic releases negotiate the relationship between abstraction and political reality with such confidence. Rather than attempting to sonically represent conflict, first quarter of 21st century insists that the listener complete the work themselves. In doing so, it transforms listening into an ethical act, where sound becomes not an illustration of history but a space in which our relationship to it is quietly, and uncompromisingly, tested. To better understand his production process we reached out directly to Pé who kindly agreed to answer four questions over an email exchange. Your earlier releases—ædæm: representations of nonexistence, æbæd: through imagining eternity, and æzæl: eternity of nonexistence—were concerned with philosophical questions of time, existence, and cosmology, often expressed through abstract titles and long-form synthesizer improvisations. Beginning with gold bars made in dubai, which confronted the war in Sudan through the global trade in gold, and continuing with 40.8 tonnes of freedom and now first quarter of 21st century, your work has become increasingly explicit in its engagement with contemporary conflicts and political violence. What prompted this shift? Do you see these recent releases as a rupture with your earlier work, or do they emerge from the same philosophical concerns viewed through the realities of the present? To start with what has prompted the shift from philosophical topics to contemporary conflicts; it was an attempt to moving towards “transdisciplinary approach” and progressing from – so called – philosophical thought experiments, by borrowing from journalism. therefore i am a bit reluctant to view these projects as a rupture from past practices rather than some form of evolution, since they are still a call for attention to “ignorance”. The titles of first quarter of 21st century—”82,448 palestinians”, “conservatively confirmed death toll”, and “courtesy of state of israel”—leave no room for ambiguity. Yet the music itself remains instrumental, refusing illustration or overt emotional cues. What relationship were you hoping to establish between these stark factual titles and the abstract electronic sound world? Did you want listeners to experience the tension between documentation and interpretation rather than being directed toward a single emotional response? The refusal of illustration and a directed emotional response, as you mentioned, is the manner which I appreciate most in art, regardless of form/field; for its insistence on self reflection that the audience should bear. Trying to sonically represent (in the tone discussed) what the title says, or to be more precise the gap between them, would be filled by the audience confronting their stance, personally or culturally, on the subject. Across your discography there is a striking consistency in your working methods: extreme frequencies, minimal editing, the recurring use of the ARP Odyssey, and an emphasis on limitation as a compositional principle. Even as the conceptual focus has shifted from metaphysics to contemporary history, your sonic language has remained remarkably coherent. What continues to attract you to these self-imposed constraints? Do they allow you to respond to radically different subjects without changing your musical vocabulary? The self-imposed constraints are mostly for avoiding redundancy as well as driving creativity. Of course the personal preferences of frequency ranges, prepared signal chains and doing the least in DAW, are still shaping much of the sonic characteristics. Although, the limitations of choosing ARP Odyssey module as the sole source might be too many, its availability is what makes it convenient enough for now. Combining all these has given me access to some sort of primal sonic vocabulary (in my opinion) which leaves plenty room for expression in the manner discussed before, regardless of topic. You are an Iranian artist releasing music at a moment when questions of war, state violence, displacement, and historical memory don’t just affect you personally but resonate across the region. gold bars made in dubai, 40.8 tonnes of freedom, and first quarter of 21st century all engage with different conflicts while avoiding overt musical illustration. Do you think artists have a responsibility to bear witness to political reality, or is your work simply a personal response to living through the first quarter of the twenty-first century? Subjects of the releases you mentioned can be described as “shrugged off crimes against humanity”, and the responsibility of paying attention to these – and the normalized ignorance towards them – does not fall upon a certain group; bearing or avoiding these responsibilities can be rooted in different aspects of one’s identity and principles, as well as their dedication to cling to the bubble they live in. In short, the answer to this question is both, responsibility as an artist, and personal response as a witness. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Desde cuando te pregunto si tuyo puedo ser? Hace tiempo que no siento fallo por no perder No lamento lo que no pude tener Solo arrepiento mirarte y saber Five albums into Casual Confrontation, Frankie Diez has decided that refinement is overrated when you can instead build a nightclub out of sheet metal, subwoofers, bad memories, and one unwelcome face in the crowd. ARREBATO, the first single from the forthcoming BASTION, takes reggaeton’s dembow gait and marches it straight into industrial machinery, where darkwave synths hover overhead, and the breakdowns come down with Ministry-sized force. The title means “rapture,” and Diez draws part of its charge from Iván Zulueta’s 1979 Spanish arthouse horror film Arrebato, a movie where obsession becomes appetite and starts swallowing people. This song is about the moment attention curdles into surveillance. Somebody from years ago keeps turning up where the singer goes, particularly in the dark club where being found feels less romantic than invasive. Desire has crossed a line, and Diez answers with disgust sharp enough to leave teeth marks. The bilingual chorus gives the confrontation force because the switch into English lands with the plainness of somebody abandoning diplomacy. There is no ornate misery here, no candlewax poetry about doomed lovers circling each other forever. The emotional center is recognition: realizing that another person has interpreted access as entitlement, then saying the ugly necessary words aloud. Musically, Diez has identified a seemingly obvious combination that, in hindsight, raises the question of why more artists haven’t explored it. Reggaeton already employs repetition as a form of physical persuasion, while EBM and industrial music have long integrated themes of menace, machinery, and bodily discipline. By layering the dembow rhythm, typical of Bad Bunny, beneath synth textures reminiscent of Ultra Sunn, and allowing the track to develop a metallic impact similar to what Ministry once emphasized as a civic duty, “Reggaeton Gótico” transitions from seeming like a joke made at closing time to presenting a viable, compelling concept. Diez explains the connection through experience rather than genre theory: “I always listened to reggaeton growing up in both Puerto Rico and in Miami, and the genre fusion always felt natural, since much of reggaeton can easily have somewhat of a dark-clubbing atmosphere already.” That background keeps ARREBATO from feeling like two record collections stapled together. The rhythm sits inside the song’s bloodstream, while the harsher electronic elements intensify its sense of danger. By the breakdown, the club has become a pressure chamber and the confrontation feels public, which may be the point: stalkers thrive on ambiguity, private fear, and the hope that their target will remain polite. Watch the lyric video below: ARREBATO ends that politeness. If BASTION follows this path, Casual Confrontation may have stumbled onto a nasty little hybrid with real legs: music for dancing, recoiling, and finally telling somebody who will not take the hint exactly where the door is. Listen to ARREBATO below and order the single here. items.body: When Thomas Rainer and I spoke in 2024, “Verboten!” was presented as a decisive stage in Nachtmahr’s development, a record moving the project toward something more mature and less interested in obeying its own established rules. Two years later, Rainer slightly revises that interpretation himself: “Verboten!” did not complete an evolution, it established the method for what came next. That next step is “IMPERIVM”, released on June 26, 2026, ten tracks in which ideas first tested on “Verboten!” are refined rather than simply repeated. Between the two records came “Dominant: The Piano Sessions”, apparently moving in the opposite direction by removing much of Nachtmahr’s electronic machinery and exposing the construction underneath. Rainer, however, sees the piano record as a separate exercise, one intended to demonstrate something he considers fundamental: beneath the production, the songs have to survive. “IMPERIVM” then returns to force, rhythm and electronics with that confidence already established. The title creates another, more interesting complication. “IMPERIVM” inevitably suggests command, hierarchy and centralised authority, ideas that already sit comfortably within Nachtmahr’s visual vocabulary. Rainer’s interpretation is different. The Empire here is the relationship between the project and the people who have sustained it; many of the record’s lyrical ideas were informed by their experiences. Resistance, in his account, is not presented as party politics but as resistance to conformity, exclusion and the pressure to become easier to categorise. That tension becomes particularly clear when Nachtmahr moves from record to stage. The upcoming “IMPERIVM” tour is being presented as the project’s longest and largest to date, with Cygnosic and Bagger 258 joining the tour; the first three dates take place in Poland, in Wrocław, Poznań and Warsaw, before the itinerary continues through Austria and Germany. What looks like excess from the audience side is, Rainer explains, built on considerable precision behind it. The starting point is not the lighting, uniforms or visuals, but the setlist. Everything else follows its dramaturgy. We spoke about what “Verboten!” actually changed, why stripping Nachtmahr down to piano mattered, the meaning behind “IMPERIVM”, politics and the limits of artistic influence, the paradox of creating a safe space through an aesthetic built around hierarchy and discipline, the scene’s attachment to nostalgia, and why losing control onstage requires a great deal of control everywhere else. Karo: When we spoke in 2024, you described “Verboten!” as the album that would complete Nachtmahr’s evolution toward a more mature, less playful sound, and you said its release would herald a new era for the project. Two years later, “IMPERIVM” is already here. Looking back, was “Verboten!” actually the arrival point you imagined at the time, or did making that record reveal another direction you had not yet anticipated? Thomas: “Verboten!” was not the album that completed an evolution, but it set the course for the future. It was a successful experiment that paved the way for the sound and writing of “IMPERIVM”. Many techniques and structural improvements were first introduced during the production of “Verboten!” and then refined, expanded and improved for its successor. Karo: Between “Verboten!” and “IMPERIVM” came “Dominant: The Piano Sessions”, reducing Nachtmahr material to piano before you returned with something considerably more forceful and electronic. That is an interesting sequence: first removing much of the machinery, then rebuilding it at full pressure. What did you discover about your own songwriting when rhythm, distortion and production were stripped away? Did any of that feed back into the way you approached “IMPERIVM”? Thomas: The piano album was a standalone project and can be seen more as a sister concept to the acoustic releases “Flamme”, “Funke” and “Feuer”, as they all follow the same idea: deconstructing and rebuilding Nachtmahr’s music to showcase aspects of the compositions that were overlooked before. Ultimately, they proudly proclaim that our music also works in a stripped-down version because, in its essence, these are simply good songs. Something that most bands in our scene couldn’t achieve. Karo: “IMPERIVM” is a loaded title. Empire suggests hierarchy, command and centralised power, while the record is framed around resistance, nonconformity and refusing to be broken. Nachtmahr has always borrowed the language and aesthetics of authority while often directing the content somewhere much less obedient. Has that contradiction become more central now: the possibility of appropriating the appearance of power in order to question power itself? Thomas: “IMPERIVM”, both as an album and as a title, is a monument to our incredible fan base that has carried us on its wings over the years, through light and shadow. Our fans and us, indivisible and forged together in fire and flame, are an Empire. An army is nothing without a commander, and vice versa. This is what the title stands for. Karo: Taken together, titles such as “Unterwerfung”, “Willenlos”, “Stärker als ihr Hass” and “Neue Ufer” seem to establish a tension between submission and refusal, being acted upon and reclaiming agency. Is there a movement through “IMPERIVM” from one condition toward the other, or are you more interested in the uncomfortable fact that power and submission can coexist inside the same person? Thomas: It is hard to find a common denominator for all the titles you mentioned, as they all have very different meanings and intentions, both lyrically and musically. One common theme remains, though. As I already explained in relation to the title, the red thread binding all the songs together is the connection between our fans and us. It was their stories and experiences that inspired me when writing the lyrics. That ranges from “Stärker als ihr Hass”, which is a strong statement for self-expression against all external factors, to “Unterwerfung”, which deals with self-discovery in a BDSM context. Karo: In our previous conversation, you were very precise about one boundary: you said that the influence an artist receives from an audience creates a responsibility not to turn that power into political endorsement. At the same time, the language around “IMPERIVM” now invokes resistance, solidarity and revolution. Has that boundary become harder to maintain? When does resistance remain an artistic or existential idea, and when does an audience inevitably begin to read it politically? Thomas: There is still no political statement whatsoever. We praise individuality, self-discovery and self-expression above all. There is resistance against social norms, solidarity with those oppressed for expressing themselves, and revolution against a system that wants to keep people conforming and alike because that makes them easier to rule, steer and oppress. This has nothing to do with politics per se, but with things everybody can change or take action on themselves. Karo: The current presentation of Nachtmahr also speaks about the project as a space for outsiders and people who do not comfortably fit social norms. That creates an intriguing tension with a visual vocabulary built around severity, uniforms, hierarchy and control. Is that paradox important to you? Can a space feel safe precisely because everybody inside it understands that the threatening imagery belongs to an artistic construction rather than an actual hierarchy between the people in the room? Thomas: There is a paradox, but that is exactly the point. The uniforms, hierarchy and discipline are part of the artistic world of Nachtmahr, not a real hierarchy between the people in the room. Quite the opposite: everyone enters that world on equal terms. I think that is why it can, and should, feel liberating. Everybody knows that the threatening imagery is theatre, and that gives people the freedom to step outside their everyday roles for a while, perhaps even discovering their true selves in the process. Karo: In 2024, you told me that Nachtmahr’s success had finally given you enough confidence to stop caring about the stylistic boundaries of the scene and to give each song whatever treatment it required. After almost 20 years, is crossing genre boundaries still liberating, or has the more difficult challenge become escaping the conventions of your own musical language? Thomas: After so many years, you can easily start repeating your own formula. “IMPERIVM” was about avoiding that. Every song should sound the way that song needs to sound, even if that means stepping outside the Nachtmahr rulebook, if there even is one. The scene we mostly operate in thrives on nostalgia, and it would be easy, and maybe even more successful, to keep repeating that formula. But my own artistic standards make me want to reinvent over and over. Karo: The new tour is being presented as something much larger than simply performing songs from “IMPERIVM”: sound, visuals, outfits, light and attitude functioning together as one system. When you construct a Nachtmahr show now, where does that process begin? With the music, with an image, with the physical reaction you want from the audience, or does the performance only really exist once all those elements begin influencing one another? Thomas: Every tour design begins with the setlist. This is the key. Once the dramaturgy is established, all the other elements follow suit. The setlist is the script for the movie we present every night on tour, adapted to the local circumstances. It is a short answer and it may sound simple, but trust me: getting the setlist right takes weeks and can make or break every show, no matter how good the other elements are. Karo: You are opening this tour with three nights in Poland, Wrocław, Poznań and Warsaw. There is something appealing about beginning a large production in club rooms where the distance between performer and audience is relatively small. Does starting in Poland carry any particular significance for you, and what do those first nights need to tell you before the rest of the tour unfolds? Thomas: Starting the tour in Poland was a logistical decision at first, but in the end it is the perfect kick-off for what we plan to bring to the stage. Judging from my previous experiences in Poland, the crowds are very enthusiastic and welcoming. On the other hand, there are always certain insecurities within the band when you present a new programme for the first time. I am 100 percent sure all of those will be swept away by the energy of our Polish fans, and that wave will carry us all the way through the other dates of the tour. Karo: Cygnosic and Bagger 258 are joining you on the tour and bring rather different approaches to electronic physicality. When you choose touring partners, do you think primarily in terms of compatible audiences, or about the architecture of the entire evening? Can the support acts change the state in which the audience eventually receives Nachtmahr? Thomas: Good support acts are very important for how every night goes. They can make it easier or harder for the main act when they enter the stage; for example, a well-warmed-up crowd is already at a point that you would normally need to take them to yourself. The main factor in whom I take on tour is a personal one, though. I want to tour with people I genuinely like and who share the same morals and work ethic as my team and me. You know what they say, “one bad apple can spoil the whole basket”, and this is very true on tour. I speak from experience. Karo: There is a fundamental contradiction in Nachtmahr live that becomes more interesting as the production grows. On your side of the stage, enormous control is required: sound, light, visuals and presentation have to work together. Yet what the performance seems to seek from the audience is almost the reverse: surrender, physical release, catharsis. How much control do you need to exercise in order to create a space where everybody else can safely lose theirs? Thomas: I have a wonderful band and crew who take the need for control out of my hands, so I can completely let go onstage and simply become one with the energy of the crowd, opening the floodgates of my heart and letting all my emotions pour out. The same is true for the crowd. They should completely lose themselves in the music. The safe space you mentioned can only partly be created by us. Mostly responsible for that is our wonderful fan base, which is accepting and welcoming to everyone, and of course the great promoters of each show, who also do their part. Karo: This is being presented as the largest and longest Nachtmahr tour so far. Rather than asking what people can “expect” from it, I’m more interested in what you expect to discover. After almost two decades of Nachtmahr, what can a tour of this scale still teach you about the project that you do not already know, and which of the coming shows are you personally most curious to experience? Thomas: Honestly, I am mostly curious about discovering my most recent songs in a live context, performing them and maybe falling in love with them all over again. I want to see which parts of which songs resonate with whom in the crowd. And secondly, I am looking forward to hanging out with and meeting our fans. Nachtmahr tour dates 2026 1 October 2026 – Wrocław, Poland – Klub Łącznik 2 October 2026 – Poznań, Poland – Klub Pod Minogą 3 October 2026 – Warsaw, Poland – VooDoo Club 17 October 2026 – Vienna, Austria – Escape Metalcorner 5 November 2026 – Munich, Germany – Backstage 6 November 2026 – Nuremberg, Germany – Der Cult 14 November 2026 – Hamburg, Germany – Logo 15 November 2026 – Berlin, Germany – Frannz Club 27 November 2026 – Erfurt, Germany – Club From Hell 28 November 2026 – Dresden, Germany – Strasse E 4 December 2026 – Oberhausen, Germany – Kulttempel 5 December 2026 – Mannheim, Germany – MS Connexion Complex 12 December 2026 – Aarburg, Switzerland – Musigburg About Nachtmahr Nachtmahr is the Austrian industrial electronic project founded by Thomas Rainer in 2007. Beginning with the “Kunst ist Krieg” EP, Rainer developed a deliberately severe musical and visual language built around hard electronic rhythms, distorted club structures, uniforms, discipline, sexuality, confrontation and theatricalised images of authority. Over almost two decades, the project has expanded from Rainer’s original conception into a full live band. Its catalogue now encompasses eleven studio albums and nine EPs, alongside extensive international touring. While Nachtmahr is frequently situated within industrial, EBM and dark electronic music, Rainer has increasingly resisted treating those categories as compositional limits. Recent releases illustrate that widening vocabulary particularly clearly. “Verboten!” arrived in 2024, followed in 2025 by “Dominant: The Piano Sessions”, which reinterpreted Nachtmahr material through piano arrangements. “IMPERIVM”, released on June 26, 2026 through Trisol Music Group, returns to the project’s electronic force while developing the compositional and structural ideas Rainer says were first tested on “Verboten!”. The album contains ten tracks, including “Wer Wind sät”, “Unterwerfung”, “Stärker als ihr Hass”, “Willenlos” and “Neue Ufer”. Interview by Karo Kratochwil.
items._cn_summary: Nachtmahr的新专辑《IMPERIVM》延续了前作《Verboten!》确立的方法论，将实验性的声音设计与更为成熟的创作方向结合。乐队主脑Thomas Rainer在访谈中强调，专辑标题并非指向集权或等级，而是象征着项目与听众之间的紧密联结，歌词灵感多来自支持者的真实经历。在《Dominant: The Piano Sessions》中剥离电子机械、以钢琴暴露歌曲骨架之后，这张专辑回归了力量、节奏与电子声响，并带着已被验证的自信。舞台呈现方面，巡演以歌单为叙事核心，灯光、制服与视觉均围绕其戏剧结构展开，在看似过度的表象下依赖精确的控制。访谈还涉及对顺从、排斥与分类压力的抵抗，以及如何在以纪律为美学基础的形式中创造安全空间。整体上，这是一张在工业暗潮框架内继续深化个人语言的作品，兼具冲击力与思考深度。

items.body: For nearly two decades now, Providence-based artist Tomas Bennett has been making some of the most uncompromising harsh noise in the game as Tinnitustimulus. In addition to following through on the project’s eponymous promise—most of his work features frequencies that will shred your eardrums if you’re not careful—Bennett has always been inclined toward long, droning compositions that induce a punishing kind of hypnosis. You can hear this interest as far back as 2015’s Roquefort, but it’s especially present on recent releases like Omnipresence and Vortices. It dovetails with a parallel interest in stripping down his setup, which these days often consists of a laptop, an interface, and a mixer. Accordingly, the back of the O-card for Fountain, the first tape on a new presumably in-house imprint Fecund, frankly states that “No acoustic feedback was used in these recordings.” Both sides are filled with undammed, unbroken surges of noise, almost numbing in their monolithic monotony. The commitment to sustained feedback studies reminds me of the Agitant Group tape on Head Meat from last year, but of course this is strictly digital. That being said, the analog presentation softens the edges a bit, slathering a topcoat of murk that serves as a nice complement to the serrated layers as they phase in and out. Somehow Bennett always knows the perfect moments to tweak his overloaded systems so that they start to thrash and fracture, threatening to tear themselves apart but never quite breaking the surface tension of the relentless current—that is, until the very end of the B side, which makes it all the more satisfying. Copies are available via email: tinnitustimulus@yahoo.com.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是普罗维登斯噪音艺术家托马斯的全新磁带作品，也是其新厂牌的首个发行。两面各是一段不间断的噪音洪流，以数字方式生成的持续反馈为基底，完全没有使用声学反馈。作者近年精简为笔记本、声卡和调音台的配置，在这部作品中体现为近乎催眠的单调压迫感。磁带媒介为锋利刺耳的锯齿层次蒙上一层浑浊质感，使声音在相位漂移中不断变化。他总能在恰当时刻扭动过载系统，让噪音开始剧烈震荡、濒临崩裂，却始终不破坏持续电流的表面张力，直到第二面结尾才终于释放，带来满足的收束。

items.excerpt: Teranga is a Wolof word for hospitality, the welcome extended to a guest. Wau Wau Collectif named their third album after it, and after years of building songs remotely, this is the record where the band finally met in person. “Oh Africa!” is the second single from it. The Swedish-Senegalese project runs on files traded over WhatsApp. Karl-Jonas Winqvist in Sweden and Arouna Kane in Senegal started it in Toubab Dialaw in 2018, a fishing and artist village on Senegal’s Petite Cô
items.body: Teranga is a Wolof word for hospitality, the welcome extended to a guest. Wau Wau Collectif named their third album after it, and after years of building songs remotely, this is the record where the band finally met in person. “Oh Africa!” is the second single from it. The Swedish-Senegalese project runs on files traded over WhatsApp. Karl-Jonas Winqvist in Sweden and Arouna Kane in Senegal started it in Toubab Dialaw in 2018, a fishing and artist village on Senegal’s Petite Côte, about 60 kilometres south of Dakar. The town has long drawn dancers, musicians and sculptors. From there the pair built a network that grew to 26 musicians and songwriters across three albums. Teranga was finished and mixed on the group’s first tour, five weeks across Europe with, as Winqvist puts it, “three Swedes, three Senegalese, and a French driver”. “Oh Africa!” turns on a winding guitar line with an almost Turkish bend, the kind of riff that could pass for a lost cut on a decades-old reissue. It comes third on Teranga, where the collective sets balafon, ngoni and calabash against violin, cello, saxophone and Omnichord. Winqvist has named Barney Wilen‘s Moshi, the French saxophonist’s 1972 album built from recordings made during his travels in Africa, as an influence. Released by Sahel Sounds, Teranga closes the trilogy that began with Yaral Sa Doom and Mariage, though Winqvist says the band have “barely started in some ways”, with more touring planned. Stream “Oh Africa!” and pre-order Teranga via THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Wau Wau Collectif – Oh Africa! appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._cn_summary: 瑞典与塞内加尔音乐人通过WhatsApp远程协作，集结26位乐手完成第三张专辑《Teranga》，单曲《Oh Africa!》以蜿蜒的吉他线融合土耳其式弯音，并搭配巴拉丰、恩戈尼与卡拉巴什等西非传统乐器，同时引入小提琴、大提琴、萨克斯与Omnichord，形成跨大陆的声响对话。作品灵感源自法国萨克斯手Barney Wilen在非洲旅行录音的1972年专辑《Moshi》，在当代世界音乐语境中延续了非洲与欧洲即兴传统的交融。专辑在乐队首次欧洲巡演期间完成混音，由独立厂牌Sahel Sounds发行，体现出在地合作与远程创作结合下的独特文化视角。

items.body:
First solo album from Tokyo pianist and composer Kotaro Maruyama - constructed entirely from the sound source of the OP-Z digital synthesizer in a single take.

"Composing primarily with the piano, Kotaro Maruyama creates music for a variety of visual media, including commercials and short films. Influenced by the composer Toru Takemitsu, he places importance on the “silence” and "ambience" of sound, aiming to create works where the music quietly depicts a scene.

Kotaro Maruyama's first solo album, "Vapor Curve," is constructed entirely from the sound source of the OP-Z digital synthesizer. Notably, he avoids the concept of harmony for a single tone, instead pursuing a unique "woven harmony" created by intricately layering multiple independent melodies. Using only the OP-Z, and recording everything in a single take without using a computer, Kotaro Maruyama's "Vapor Curve" is distinguished by its uncompromising production style. The minimalist melodies that are layered to create an ambient soundscape, along with the incidental noise that gives an organic texture to the inorganic electronic sound, showcase the raw appeal of sound that is imperfect."
items._cn_summary: 东京钢琴家与作曲家丸山公太的首张个人专辑，完全以一台数字合成器为音源，并在不使用电脑的情况下一次性录制完成。受武满彻影响，他重视声音中的“寂静”与“氛围”，拒绝围绕单一音调构建和声，而是通过精细叠置多条独立旋律形成独特的“编织和声”。极简旋律铺展出环境音景，偶然杂音为无机电子声响注入有机质感，使作品带有未加修饰的原始听感。整张专辑以极简的制作手段呈现了声音本身的质感与过程性。

items.body:
One of the UK’s most distinctive filmmakers returns to the sea, replete with his original synth score - as on ‘Bait’ and ‘Enys Men’ - but notably damper, deeply blue; surely evoking fellow Cornish native AFX’s ‘SAW II’, BoC interludes, Mordant Music, classic folk horror OSTs.

Centred around the tale of a trawler that returns, sans crew, to a Cornish harbour years after it was thought lost, ‘The Rose Of Nevada’ typically draws on what Mark Jenkin knows best - the people, places and metaphysics of the Atlantic peninsula - whilst ideally emphasising the atmosphere with his special ingredient score. His palette of tape-smudged analog synths feels especially washed out and suggestive of his subject in its briny tone and oceanic scale, which evidently works a treat as a discrete work in its own right, severed from imagery. 

There’s possibly a Kernewek word for “hiraeth”, or “sehnsucht” - a sense of longing, nostalgia - that we’re not aware of, but may perfectly fit the feeling of Jenkin’s music here. Sea-legged loops and sustained drones colour the air with a palpable melancholy in passage from the bittersweet tang of ‘Kneebone Barton’, as used on the trailer, and throughout the album’s patches of decaying wheeze, staining the surface like rust or efflorescence on weathered coves. 

And in the day-dreamiest sense it all fades in/out of consciousness with a perfectly ghostly wow and flutter, as leaching from ‘Through The Gaps’ parts into the slurred whorl of ‘What’s Your Name,’ ephemeral concrète of ‘Look At It’, and final folksy shuffle off into the horizon with ‘Rose of Nevada.’ Here’s looking forward to the film.

items._cn_summary: Mark Jenkin为电影《The Rose Of Nevada》创作的原声配乐，延续了他在《Bait》和《Enys Men》中标志性的磁带模拟合成器手法，但整体氛围更加湿润深沉，带有浓烈的海洋气息与蓝色忧郁感。乐评指出，音乐通过循环音型与持续低音构建出类似hiraeth的怀旧与乡愁情绪，音色经过磁带磨损处理，仿佛被海水浸蚀，呈现出锈迹与风化般的质感。作品融合了民俗恐怖片原声的经典元素，同时令人联想到AFX、Boards of Canada等电子音乐人的氛围段落，在梦境般的恍惚感中，以缓慢的渐变与抖动贯穿始终。即使脱离影像，这张专辑也能作为独立的氛围电子作品成立，在听觉上营造出幽灵般缥缈的航海叙事。

items.body:
Deep club modernist Sa Pa mints his own new label, Dub Techno For Life, with four top drawer cuts of textured, strident pressure tipped FFO classic Chain Reaction x Short Span.

Since 2015 Sa Pa has carved a heads-down path between techno, proper, and its conceptual adjuncts in ambient and sound designer atmospheres, most recently on Short Span and Astral Industries. Now taking matters into his own hands, the ‘Girls on Tour EP’ squares up his most robust club material alongside more experimental urges for a definitive self-portrait displaying a fine spectrum of strengths. 

The four tunes clearly speak to his diversity within a theme, checking for a firm touchstone in Andreas Tilliander aka Mokira with the 10 mins of rolling, claggy heft to ‘Mokira Ultra Dub’, unshelving his 2016 rework for deep ’26 ‘floors, alongside the puckered elegance of ‘Waiting For You’, harking to roots in Teutonic house minimalism, whereas the B-side attends to grubbier urges in the bittersweet, sludgy budge of ‘Modular System’, and lusher, abstract feels on the Actress or Rezzett-esque whorl of ‘World Saving Banger’.
items._genre: dub techno / minimal techno / ambient / electronic
items._cn_summary: 萨帕在自创厂牌下推出这张四曲唱片，把俱乐部舞曲的冲击力与氛围化声音设计并置。前半部分以十余分钟厚重滚动的《莫基拉超级混音》向瑞典电子音乐人安德烈亚斯·蒂利安德致敬，延续柏林式回响科技舞曲的质感；《等待你》则带有德式浩室极简的优雅。后半部分转向更粗粝的表达，《模块系统》在苦涩而泥泞的律动中推进，《拯救世界的劲曲》呈现类似英国抽象电子艺人的回旋纹理。整张唱片在科技舞曲、极简与氛围之间穿行，既是舞池材料，也是声音实验的自我写照。

items.body:
Munich’s modern art gallery Museum Brandhorst field wide ranging responses to an exhibit of works and concerts focussed on the works of John Cage, Merce Cunningham, Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg and Cy Twombly, ranging from the sound poetry of Sofia Biazzi; to the sublime levitations of Maria Margolina; avant ambient pop of water lily; the pulsating technoid attack of focus baby; andCaroline Kretschmer’s subaquatic intrigue.

“Museum Brandhorst has invited Sound and Experiment to create a series of performances, audio works, and concerts in relation to the exhibition Fünf Freunde: John Cage, Merce Cunningham, Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg, Cy Twombly. The event took place on June 27, 2025, as part of the Junge Nacht and the opening night of the annual Kunstareal Fest in Munich. The program featured newly produced pieces by Sound and Experiment participants Sofian Biazzi, Ilinca Fechete, focus baby, Daniel Gianfranceschi, Bruno Haas, Caroline Kretschmer, Bradley Leonard, Camilla Metelka, Maria Margolina, rosi and water lily. 

In a preparatory, biweekly seminar, discussions addressed conditions such as spectrotemporal displays, sharing time and frequency domains with different sound pieces simultaneously, and eventual performance constellations. An additional point of departure was a close reading of the indirect role of American artist David Tudor in some of the positions exhibited in Fünf Freunde, the function of the organization E.A.T. (Experiments in Art and Technology), and auditory scene analysis and synthesis in general.

The pieces featured on this CD are related to the presented performances, yet newly produced and with the audio CD format in mind.”

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑源自慕尼黑现代美术馆围绕约翰·凯奇、默斯·坎宁安等艺术家展览所策划的系列演出与声音项目，参与者在研讨中探讨了频谱时间展示、多作品同时共享时间与频率域等概念，并参考了大卫·图德与E.A.T.组织的间接影响。最终收录的曲目并非现场录音，而是为CD介质重新创作的声音作品。整体涵盖声音诗、氛围悬浮感、前卫氛围流行、脉冲式电子攻击性以及水下般的细腻声响，呈现出从抽象声音实验到节奏驱动电子乐的广泛光谱，体现了当代声音艺术与音乐创作之间的流动边界。作品在概念构架与声响材质上都具备鲜明的实验性，适合关注声音艺术、前卫电子与跨媒介创作的听众。

items.body:
Marco Cassanelli's latest four-track EP in deep, atmospheric dub techno.

"Rich in warmth, texture and groove, the release finds the Italian producer at his most refined, effortlessly balancing hypnotic rhythms with expansive chord work and immersive sound design that resonates equally on the dancefloor and in more introspective home listening settings.

For more than two decades, Marco Cassanelli has been quietly refining a sound rooted in the deepest traditions of dub techno. Emerging from Rome’s underground electronic scene, he has built a body of work defined by patience, restraint, and a profound understanding of space and atmosphere.

Each track unfolds with patience and purpose, drawing listeners into a world of drifting echoes, subtle movement and finely crafted detail. Rooted firmly in the traditions of dub techno while retaining a distinctive character of its own, the EP is both deeply engaging and beautifully understated—equally suited to late-night club systems and home listening.

The final track introduces an unexpected vocal performance, adding a fresh dimension to the release and bringing the journey to a memorable close.Elegant, timeless and richly textured, this EP is a testament to Cassanelli’s enduring craftsmanship and his ability to create dub techno of the highest calibre."
items._cn_summary: 这张四轨EP延续了Marco Cassanelli二十年来的沉静美学，以深邃、温暖的氛围化律动为核心。作品在催眠式节奏与宽广和弦之间取得平衡，声音设计细腻且富有空间感，既适合俱乐部深夜场景，也适合居家专注聆听。每首曲目以耐心铺陈的方式展开，漂移的回声与微妙的动态变化构建出沉浸式听觉旅程。最后一曲意外引入人声，为整体氛围增添新的维度，并以记忆点收束全篇。整体上，EP根植于dub techno传统，同时保留鲜明的个人辨识度，制作精致而不张扬，展现出作者对空间、留白与细节的成熟掌控，属于该领域内质感上乘的佳作。

items.body:
Beirut-based sound artist and veteran improviser Jad Atoui captures his country's current instability on his latest full-length, performing live in situ with his modular rig.

Ostensibly a noise record, it's inspired by Atoui's early club experiences, where he twigged the physicality of sound for the first time. Here, he uses the same properties to provoke very different responses, layering distorted waves of sound on 'Pressure Dream' that might as well be collapsing buildings. And by recording the material live, there's a distinct human touch that's often missing from this kind of material. Atoui is able to work instinctively, reacting to the sound in the room on the outstanding 'Reaching Heart' as glassy drones bend to corroded rhythmic interjections. 

There's even a glimmer of hope; the gorgeous 'Blue Moon Red Cloud' is a break from stuttering beats and searing noise that hits like an oasis in the desert, lifted by Atoui's freeform melodies and delirious FM chimes.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以贝鲁特当下的动荡为背景，由声音艺术家在实地以模块化合成器现场录制。表面上是噪音作品，但灵感来自早期俱乐部体验中对声音物理性的感知，因此噪音并非抽象暴力，而是带有身体与空间感。录音保留即兴触感，演奏者能对房间中的声响做出即时反应，如《Reaching Heart》中玻璃般的长音与腐蚀性节奏穿插；《Pressure Dream》的失真声浪被形容为近乎崩塌的建筑。专辑并非一味尖锐，也有《Blue Moon Red Cloud》这样以自由旋律和FM钟琴音色构成的绿洲式段落，在急促节拍与灼热噪音之间提供喘息。整体上它以现场性、即兴性和文化语境区别于同类噪音电子作品。

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是IDM先驱The Black Dog的ambient作品，以巡游记忆中的场所为核心概念——那些被自然吞没的童年故地，以及已变成新住宅区的旧日土地。乐评指出，这一主题会向每位听者提出不同的想象课题，使聆听体验带有强烈的个人化色彩。结尾曲《Every Empty Room》中低沉的节拍被描述为能让人联想到一束光，为整张专辑留下充满希望的余韵。整体上，作品以环境声响构建回忆与变迁的氛围，兼具概念性与情绪感染力。

items.body: Label: Biophilia Records, 2026 Personnel - Linda May Han Oh: double bass; Melissa Aldana: tenor saxophone. Bassist Linda May Han Oh and saxophonist Melissa Aldana are two respected bandleaders and composers with different styles and approaches but common journeys in life. Oh was born in Malaysia to parents of Chinese heritage, was raised in Australia, and moved to New York for a brilliant career, having played with Pat Metheny, Vijay Iyer, Joe Lovano, and Dave Douglas, among many others. Aldana is a native of Santiago, Chile, and has lived in New York since 2009, after graduating from Berklee College of Music. For this session, the duo agreed to play standards, showcasing reverence for jazz tradition and influences while also allowing new possibilities to emerge from the arrangements. Yet Beneath Lifted Skies also includes three duo improvisations and three solo bass tracks. Charlie Parker’s “ Anthropology ” comes out of the gate with a vibrantly swinging mood, swift unisons, and exciting exchanges infused with a richness of ideas. Yet it doesn’t beat the fantastic rendition of Bud Powell’s “ Hallucinations ”, where the duo is at its best. Impressive synchronization, great melody, and a grooving, energizing vibe are part of a breathtaking interplay that demonstrates Oh’s immaculate technique and Aldana’s fluid language. Ballads where melody reigns, such as Charles Mingus’ “ Duke Ellington’s Sound of Love ” and Sammy Fain’s “ I’ll Be Seeing You ”, make a great pair. Aldana’s quick-witted, arpeggiated sequences à la Charles Lloyd put a smokiness in the air. In turn, pieces by jazz giants Wayne Shorter (“ Dance Cadaverous ”) and John Coltrane (“ 26-2 ”) didn’t impress me as much. One that really gets under the skin is Gigi Gryce’s “ Social Call ”, a graceful, easy-rolling tune expressed with joyful hookiness. Of the three improvised pieces, “ Infinite ” is the one that caught my ear instantly, relying on droning pedals and searching melodies to take us to a progressive yet atmospheric place. “ Resolve ”, which ends with a pedaling bass figure, also makes for a compelling abstract sonic painting. Oh absolutely excels on her solo reframing of Herbie Hancock’s “ The Sorcerer ”, where edginess and roundness go together, creating an almost subliminal pulse. The bassist also tackles Billie Holiday’s “ God Bless the Child ”, delivered as a protest against child abuse, and introduces a new composition, “ Winter ”, where she employs expert pulses and slides to add novelty. Demonstrating a quick-witted rapport, Oh and Aldana are two kindred spirits in conversation. They’ve already found their own voices in jazz, but together, they manage to offer a very enjoyable album with varied rhythm, groove, and breath. While old standards can sometimes feel stale, creative reinvention transforms them into a thrilling experience. Beneath Lifted Skies is an excellent case in point. Favorite Tracks: 02 - Hallucinations ► 03 - Improvisation: Infinite ► 06 - The Sorcerer ► 10 - Social Call
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是贝斯手Linda May Han Oh与萨克斯手Melissa Aldana的二重奏合作，以标准曲目为核心，同时穿插三首二重奏即兴和三首贝斯独奏。两位音乐家来自不同文化背景，但都扎根于纽约爵士圈，在演奏中展现出默契的对话感。曲目涵盖Charlie Parker、Bud Powell、Wayne Shorter、John Coltrane等人的作品，其中对《Hallucinations》的演绎以精准同步和流畅旋律见长，而《Social Call》则呈现轻松愉悦的律动。即兴段落如《Infinite》以持续低音和探索性旋律营造出渐进氛围，贝斯独奏《The Sorcerer》在锐利与圆润之间形成微妙张力。整体上，专辑在尊重爵士传统的同时，通过改编和即兴赋予旧曲新意，展现了两位艺术家在即兴互动中的灵活思维与声音控制力。

items.body: Ahead of a set at this year's Semibreve, TYGAPAW tells Finn Cliff-Hodges about their musical journey from Kingston dancehall to the electronic underground of queer New York, and proving the industry doubters wrong Photo by Eric Johnson Gearing up to release their third studio album, TYGAPAW, real name Dion McKenzie, found themselves dwelling on some depressing realisations. During their two years making the album, they had been going through a lot of personal and professional changes. There was a sudden “lack of interest” in McKenzie’s work and bookings waned, all whilst they were transitioning. Transitioning in a conservative music industry still, consciously or unconsciously, largely framed by heteronormative views and selling to a largely conservative market.  “I was in a nightmare of a... items._cn_summary: 文章围绕TYGAPAW（Dion McKenzie）第三张专辑的创作背景展开。在制作这张专辑的两年间，McKenzie经历性别转换，同时遭遇演出邀约减少和行业兴趣下降，感受到保守音乐产业对跨性别者的排斥。访谈从牙买加Kingston的dancehall源头，延伸到纽约酷儿电子地下场景，呈现其音乐如何融合加勒比节奏、俱乐部声响与个人身份叙事。面对外界质疑，McKenzie以专辑作为赋权工具，在困境中重新确立创作方向。

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — At first, I thought of describing this EP as "Fear of a blank planet's twin sister", but afterpondering and researching the EP for a while I figured that I'd need a better metaphor, so let mesay it straight and with no second guessings : "Nil recurring" (2007) is FoaBP's extension, a sortof limb that our musical surgeon Steven Wilson removed from the regular album.Now this EP has quite a particular story, when the original "Fear of a blank planet" CD was releasedin 2007, there was the question of what to do with vinyl pressings, because the album was too longfor the format, eventually they settled on a double LP which was an expanded version of the album,since it included the tracks that would eventually form the "Nil recurring" EP. Eventually when PTregained the rights to their releases, Steven Wilson decided that new vinyl pressings would have thesame tracklisting as CD's, so the extra tracks were cut and the D side of the record is now justthe closing track "Sleep together". Original Tonefloat records pressings had this EP! It's a funfact.Regarding the music, there are many things that I'd say...Each one of the tracks (besides "Normal" which I'll get to later) are finished, fully fleshed outcompositions, each one with its own personality and vibe to it, therefore despite this EP consistingof songs that were not on the final cut, it holds up very well since it has internal consistency,completed tracks and takes itself *very seriously*. Each track has a cold, aggressive, angsty yetemotional tone, these are very industrial and I'd dare to say they are even darker than the songs onthe FoaBP record, they have the same compositional quality and style as the album since they wereborn out of the same sessions, so, anything that might apply to the formerly mentioned album alsoapplies here, they have around the same quality, both musically and production wise, they bothfeature our beloved Robert Fripp and "What happens now?" Is a sort of reprise for "Anesthetize",since it reutilizes riffs, time signatures and expands on the lyrics from the latter.As a guy who loves songs in progress (it's my guilty pleasure), "Normal" is by far the highlight ofthe album. It's a roughly mixed and engennireed, acoustic demo for "Sentimental", has the originallyrics, scrapped lyrics, scrapped motifs and the basic structure for what "Sentimental" would be,it's a piece of history. Yes, it can be hard to listen to, since neither Wilson or the band areplaying to their fullest and you can feel when they switch gears, studio, etc, but that's the charmof songs in progress, ain't I right?It's absolutely NOT a completionist EP, it's just as fundamental to their discography and history asany other album from their legendary "In absentia to The incident" run, it holds up by itself, andan essential EP for anyone remotely interested in heavy prog as a whole.

items._cn_summary: 这张EP出自与《恐惧空白星球》同期的录音素材，最初作为黑胶加长版附曲，后独立发行。乐评指出，其中除《正常》外的曲目都是完整且自成一体的创作，气质冷峻、侵略性强，带着焦虑与情绪化，比正式专辑更暗黑，工业感更重。作品延续了正式专辑的作曲与制作水准，并邀请罗伯特·弗里普参与；其中一首在动机、节拍与歌词上呼应专辑里的长曲，另一首则是粗略混音的声学样带，对应正式专辑中的慢歌，保留原始歌词、废弃素材和结构雏形，被视为创作过程的历史切片。整体并非凑数EP，而是乐队重要阶段中独立成立的作品，对重型前卫乐迷有文献与聆听双重价值。

items.body: Review by svetstawniichuk — I came to Space Revolver looking for a single-disc Flower Kings record after the long double albums, and this is the one I stayed with. 2000, Inside Out, about seventy-six minutes, ten tracks. Jonas Reingold is in on bass for the first time, and you feel the low end immediately. The rest of the room is Hasse Froberg on lead and backing vocals and acoustic guitar, Roine Stolt on guitar, bass and vocals, Tomas Bodin on piano, organ, Mellotron and synth, Hasse Bruniusson on percussion, and Ulf Wallander sitting in on soprano sax. Stolt still sings a great deal of this one, and he is in good voice.The record is built like a pair of bookends. I Am the Sun - Part One opens. I Am the Sun - Part Two closes. I hear them as one epic that someone split so the album can breathe in the middle. Part One is why I keep the disc. Atmospheric start, then organ and Mellotron from Bodin in full colour, then the band moving from section to section without the usual Flower Kings need to overstay. Midway they lean into a jazz-fusion pocket and Wallander's soprano actually earns its chair. It ends quieter, nylon guitar and Stolt almost speaking the last lines. If I have to pick a favourite, it is this first half of the sun.Dream On Dreamer is a short, airy vocal piece with keys and sax. I like it as a palate after the epic. It does not try to be important.Rumble Fish Twist is the instrumental I would play someone who thinks this band only writes hymns. First half busy, fusion-tight, Reingold given real space. Second half slower, more weather-report than guitar-hero, Bodin painting the way out. Together with the sun parts, this is the album's best writing.Monster Within starts like a holiday box and then turns heavy. Nightmarish vocal, a lot of left turns, a guitar melody at the end that feels like a hand on the shoulder after a bad dream. I do not always follow every joint, but I do not skip it. It is the strangest long song here, and the record would be blander without it.Then the single disc shows both its gift and its limit. Chicken Farmer Song is bright, almost pop, useful lightness after the monster, a little corny if you are not in the mood. Underdog is more dramatic, better vocal, a heavier last stretch. You Don't Know What You've Got is the ballad I would have left in the notebook: short, sweet, and thinner than the company it keeps. Slave to Money and A Kings Prayer bring the melodic guitar back. The prayer in particular is Stolt in his sincere Yes-adjacent mode, and the closing solo is one of the reasons people stay with this band even when a lyric goes soft.Part Two of I Am the Sun returns the themes with a more open, wandering heart, then lifts into the kind of synth-and-choir ending this group was born to write. I do not call the whole album a masterpiece. The middle has two or three tracks that are only good. As a single sitting, though, it is the cleanest long-form Flower Kings record I have used as a door into them: less filler than the doubles around it, Reingold already essential, and two genuine peaks. Four stars.Favorite track: I Am the Sun - Part One.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是瑞典前卫摇滚乐队THE FLOWER KINGS在2000年发行的单碟作品，时长约76分钟，共10首曲目。贝斯手Jonas Reingold首次加入，低音部分明显。结构上以《I Am the Sun》的上下两部作为首尾，中间穿插多首风格各异的曲目。上半部融合了管风琴、Mellotron与爵士融合段落，萨克斯演奏突出；下半部则更开放，以合成器和合唱结尾。器乐曲《Rumble Fish Twist》展现了紧凑的融合爵士技巧，而《Monster Within》则带有怪诞和戏剧性转折。整体在交响前卫框架内融入爵士元素，旋律性较强，但中段个别歌曲相对平淡。

items.body: Chicago post-punk band Oddysseys released their album However You Want It on 15 August 2026. The record runs 16 tracks and is out on Bandcamp with no label behind it: Christian Treon wrote, performed, engineered, mixed and paid for the whole thing in a small Chicago apartment. That method is also the record’s subject. Treon described the album as a slow transfer from head to tape: “The entire process was about taking something that existed only as an idea and slowly bringing it into the material world. One track at a time.” The album moves between guitar-led post-punk and harder electronic passages. “Shadow of a Sound” builds from a bass line, with lyrics Treon drew in part from Pindar’s Olympian Odes. “Cerbie” predates the album sessions and is the one track made with a full crew: Paul DiRico plays bass and drums and adds backing vocals, and John Barrett mixed it at Abbey Road. “Heaven Signs Clearly” shares its title with the band’s previous Bandcamp release and uses a call-and-response vocal over jagged guitars. ‘However You Want It’ tracklist “How Could You?”, “Shadow of a Sound”, “Romanticize”, “I Never Wanted Any of This”, “Can You Feel It?”, “Cerbie”, “Just a Filler”, “Time Thief”, “Activating Event”, “Heaven Signs Clearly”, “Bothered/Not Bothered”, “Bedlam”, “So Settle”, “Far Beyond, Beyond”, “Miles Apart”, “There’s Hope”. However You Want It by Oddysseys Oddysseys live dates in Chicago 19 August 2026 – Chicago, IL, United States – Beat Kitchen 23 September 2026 – Chicago, IL, United States – Cobra Lounge About Oddysseys Oddysseys formed in Boston and now operate out of Chicago, where the band describes itself on Bandcamp as “just a collective of people doing their best”. Christian Treon leads the project and handles the writing and recording; Paul DiRico contributes bass, drums and backing vocals. The band books its own shows through Oddhaus Booking and sells directly through Bandcamp and its own site, odd.band, rather than through a label. The group’s earlier Bandcamp release, “Heaven Signs Clearly”, preceded “However You Want It”, and its title track reappears on the new album. Oddysseys have played festival stages and improvised punk spaces on both coasts, and a live recap from a Boston show remains on the band’s YouTube channel. Verified detail on the band’s founding year and full early lineup has not been published. “However You Want It” is the largest release Oddysseys have issued to date, and the first they have put out since relocating to Chicago. The band play Beat Kitchen on 19 August, four days after the album landed.
items._cn_summary: 芝加哥后朋克乐队Oddysseys在无厂牌支持下，由Christian Treon于小公寓中独自完成创作、演奏、录音与混音，推出16轨专辑《However You Want It》。整张专辑以“将想法缓慢带入物质世界”为核心主题，音乐在吉他驱动的后朋克与更硬朗的电子段落之间切换。开篇曲《Shadow of a Sound》由贝斯线构建，歌词部分引用品达的《奥林匹亚颂歌》；《Cerbie》是唯一由完整阵容录制的作品，Paul DiRico负责贝斯、鼓与和声，并由John Barrett在Abbey Road完成混音；《Heaven Signs Clearly》则延续了乐队此前EP的同名曲，以呼应式人声配合锯齿状吉他。乐队自行预订演出并通过Bandcamp直销，体现了独立的DIY路径。该专辑融合后朋克与电子元素，制作背景与文学引用赋予其独特质感，值得一听。

items.body:
First re-pressing in years of Mark Ernestus & Moritz Von Oswald’s divine, final Rhythm & Sound release, heeling to tradition with a one-riddim album focussed on its carousel of roots reggae legends; Sugar Minott, Paul St. Hilaire, Willi Williams, Jah Cotton, Bobbo Shanti, and more

In 2005 Rhythm & Sound capped their holy mountain catalogue with ‘See Mi Yah’, a 7 x 7” set and LP which completed a 10 year run of inspired dub productions with their purest offering to the form. At the time, younger ears to their music would be left perplexed by the lack of instrumental variation - but any others with a little knowledge of one-riddim set traditions knew it was their ultimate ode to roots reggae fundamentals, after respectfully messing with the style & pattern across the Burial Mix 10”s (as collected in ‘w/ The Artists’), and the more radical 12” mutations of the Rhythm & Sound series, proper, since 1996 (not to mention birthing dub house-techno before that).     

Seeing off the project in fine style, Ernestus & Von Oswald gave studio time to their favourite vocalists, generating a slew of original performances displaying the range and depth of roots reggae’s elders and contemporary torch carriers on their signature backdrop of air-trodding bass and powdered dub chords. We were blessed to distribute it in the UK at the time, so many of these cuts are hard etched to the memory, from the ghostly croon of Willi Williams’ title piece thru the gruff gravitas of Bobbo Shanti, the duet between Ras Donovan & Ras Perez, and of course Sugar Minott’s mellifluous reggae soul.

In the year following ‘See Mi Yah’, Rhythm & Sound were naturally elected to edit and master a re-up of The Congos & Friends’ one-riddim album ’Fisherman Style’ for our then warehouse neighbours Blood & Fire Records, sealing their era of roots reflection by appropriately saluting the originators, in parallel to their Wackies reissue scheme, and before Ernestus (and Mark Ainley) would go on to found the more digi-devoted reissue label, Dug Out. Some 20 years of satisfaction later, time has proven this album holds its meditative weight.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Rhythm & Sound在2005年发行的最终作品，以one-riddim形式呈现，邀请Sugar Minott、Paul St. Hilaire、Willi Williams等雷鬼传奇与当代歌手，在统一节奏背景上录制原创人声。制作人Mark Ernestus与Moritz Von Oswald延续其标志性的深沉贝斯与粉末化和弦处理，将dub技术融入根源雷鬼的演唱传统，形成一种冥想式的整体氛围。专辑同时是对雷鬼根源的致敬，也是对其此前十年创作脉络的收束，后续他们还参与了The Congos的再版工程。对于关注电子音乐与雷鬼交汇的听者，这张作品在制作深度与声音统一性上具有持续吸引力。

items.body:
Peak Oil sublabel FO returns with a strong debut of late night, air-fried trip hop from Cold Light, flocking like moths to an illbient flame tipped FFO Jabu, Tricky, Sleepdial, Shell Company, Space Afrika.

Cold Light are Bristol’s Birthmark & Withdrawn, Portland’s Best Available Technology, Rael & Eldon out of London, and Hungarian CSNL. Some half a decade after a ‘Live at the Laundromat’ tape introduction, the collective unveil ‘Coldtron 2’, a sparingly sensuous slant on the lush pastures between trip hop, smoked-out dub soul and illbient jazz, inflected with the voices of Elaine Malone, Akeko and British-Nigerian sound designer Tony Onuchukwu. With remarkable restraint - especially considering so many hands are on board - they keep everything pared-back to creaking, atmospheric fundamentals for 40 minutes of smouldering storytelling, passing the torch across chapters of zoot-end poetic monologues, from stylised rap to spoken word, in a spectrum of accents speaking to the group’s far flung coordinates. 

Call it downbeat neo-noir or trip hop 2.0, the sound is clearly in thrall to the ‘90s OGs - Tricky, Portishead, Massive Attack - yet gauzily distinguished from its forebears by the production’s pall of dematerialised textures and an enervated feel for screwed subs and glimmers of sounds that emerged in trip hop’s fall-out. The Bristol night air is thick with sferic crackle and diffused sax in ’Smoke Signal’ thru the Memotone-esque eldritch of ‘Troposphere Test’, taking in a tacit nod to Mobb Deep via Tricky on the smouldering ‘Riot’, or even Civilistjävel!’s low-key electrodub in ‘Lean Wid It…’,    and Sleepdial’s slurred drums on ‘I’ve Known Fires’. But they’re most potent on ‘Fields in B’ with eight mins of smudged Rhythm & Sound steppas bass anchoring the bluest sax plumes and blunted bars, ideal for ashtray dreamers.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由来自布里斯托尔、波特兰、伦敦及匈牙利的音乐人集体创作，在trip hop、illbient、dub soul与爵士之间铺展出一片幽暗而松弛的声响地带。作品以极简的编曲和克制的制作贯穿全程，强调氛围化的纹理、低音与萨克斯的飘散，人声以说唱和念白交替出现，多口音与多地域的视角构成章节式的叙事。整体既回应了90年代trip hop经典的声音气质，又以当代电子制作中的解构手法和迷蒙质感与之拉开距离，在暗夜气息与烟雾缭绕的意象中保持沉静。适合偏好低音驱动、氛围浸染与实验性融合的听众。

items.body:
After marinading in the archive for 30 years, Regis unleashes a spicy batch of hypnotic meat motors hailing from an early crest of his powers, available for the first time.

It’s no real secret that Karl O’Connor dispensed dozens of 12”s in the late ‘90s under pseudonyms that are still coming to light. Since 2003, when his energies were more focussed on the BMB duo with Surgeon, he’s really pushed the techno framework into fascinating new shapes. But, like legion others, we’re all still here for his signature early brand of girder-strength bangers, as spotted ‘In Plain Sight’ here.

The title tune plays to his classic style of white knuckle tension and kinky canter with a discordant, panic-raising lead and warehouse-ready pound, whilst an early, EBM-tooled zinger ‘We Said No’ appears via two unreleased versions; a nastier alt. 1 galvanisation, and an August 1996 mix kitted with a rictus hi-hat backbone. 

Finally he dispenses an August 1996 mix of ‘Backwards Man’, which doesn’t appear on the EP of the same name nor on ‘Hard Eduction 1931’ sets, and fully endures on modern floors for its mind-bending, pitching lead and dead slinky, brutalist gait.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑汇集了Regis在90年代后期创作但未曾发表的早期作品，包括标题曲目以及两首未发行版本的《We Said No》和一首1996年8月混音的《Backwards Man》。标题曲延续了他标志性的紧张感与不和谐音色，以白指关节般的悬疑节奏和仓库舞池的沉重节拍推进；《We Said No》的两个版本带有明显的EBM工具性，其中八月混音版本以僵硬的踩镲骨架增强律动；《Backwards Man》则通过扭曲俯冲的旋律和冷峻机械的步态，在当代舞池中依然有效。这些作品展现了Karl O'Connor在早期高峰期的声音特质，融合了工业的粗粝与techno的驱动感，是了解其地下电子脉络的重要档案。

items.body:
Trane’s first album as bandleader surfaces on Craft Recordings’ guided reissue tour of classic jazz totems, spotlighting a vital period of modal jazz development from his years with the Prestige label, circa playing with Thelonious Monk and Miles Davis.

Recorded in May, 1957 and published in September that year, ’Coltrane’ marks the point when the great saxophonist began to transcend the acclaim of his peers for much wider recognition, with record sales numbers to follow suit. At the head of band including Red Garland on keys, Paul Chambers’ bass, Albert Heath on sticks, and Sahib Shihab’s baritone sax, Coltrane’s sound matures with a unique balance of smoky quintessence and modal experimentalism that would greatly inform jazz music in moving forward, outward.

That's all ideally illustrated on the daring modal suss of opener ‘Bakai’ with its switches between dervishing brass and angular rhythm to cooler stroll, and the contrast with its proceeding ‘Violets for your Furs’, and again in the closing couplet of ‘While My Lady Sleeps’ with its almost frenzied darts between the romantic and curiously exotic, and extended jazz-blues trip ‘Chronic Blues’.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是John Coltrane作为乐队领袖的首张作品，录制于1957年，正值他与Thelonious Monk及Miles Davis合作后的关键转型期。乐评指出，Coltrane在Prestige厂牌时期的风格在此趋于成熟，将烟雾般的经典爵士气质与模态实验性独特结合，对后续爵士乐的拓展方向产生了重要影响。开篇曲《Bakai》展现了大胆的模态探索，在旋转的铜管声部与棱角分明的节奏之间切换，并与随后舒缓的《Violets for your Furs》形成鲜明对比；结尾的《While My Lady Sleeps》在浪漫与奇异异域感之间急促穿梭，而《Chronic Blues》则呈现了延展的爵士布鲁斯旅程。整张专辑既保留了硬波普的根基，又透出向更自由方向推进的意图，是理解Coltrane音乐演进脉络的重要节点。

items.body:
Dalhous's first demo collection, originally released on Blackest Ever Black back in 2015. RIYL Ekoplekz, Christ or Forest Swords.

Officially established by Edinburgh-based duo Marc Dall and Alex Ander in 2012, the name Dalhous was really just a formality - the duo had already been working on material together, under the name Young Hunting, for years. This is the era that's properly dredged up here, compiling the demos that Ander and Dall originally compiled for an Intergalactic FM broadcast, eventually dubbing it to tape to fill a gap after the release of 'Will to be Well'. And it's good material, especially if you're interested in tracking the project's evolution. Picking up where that other notorious Scottish electronic duo left off when they wrote 'Twoism', Ander and Dall are fascinated by the kind of moods that disappeared when VHS was traded up for DVD. Not completely in thrall to B-movie soundtracks and documentary themes, Dalhous prefer to muddle their sound with rusted industrial grot, amping up the distortion and making sure the beats fall neatly off the grid. At 21 tracks, it's a lot to plow through, but it's tidy listening if you've already exhausted the duo's proper albums.

items.body:
All upward lift and kosmiche synth iridescence from Seoul’s blissed family band, back on the Far East’s leading krautrock revival label, Guruguru Brain...

“The blissed family band is back! TENGGER have always moved together, through time, space & genre. 'SKY' arrives as a new chapter: a little more still, a little more inward, while keeping all the warmth that's always been at the heart of what they do.

Embodying the band name meaning "endless sky" in Mongolian and "vast sea" in Hungarian, their 8th album 'SKY' centres on the feelings of boundless, infinite expansion. Conceived as one continuous environment rather than a collection of tracks, the album unfolds slowly through luminous synths, patient drones and Itta's breath-like vocals.

Like a soft big sky you can actually float on: 'SKY' is vast, warm, and wide open.

"Rather than a specific emotion, we hope the record opens a certain awareness — that the sky is not just something to be seen. Through it, we sense a connection to something much larger — a feeling of being linked to the wider universe. This sense of connection runs through the entire record.””
items._cn_summary: 这是首尔一支家庭乐队的第八张专辑。乐队名在蒙古语中意为“无尽的天空”，在匈牙利语中意为“广阔的海洋”，整张作品围绕无限扩展与连接的感受展开。全碟被构想为一个连续的声音环境，而非单曲集合，在缓慢推进的声响中逐步呈现，配合呼吸般的人声，营造出温暖、开阔且内敛的听感。乐队希望听众感受到天空不只是被观看的对象，而是通过声音与更大的宇宙产生关联。相比以往，这张作品更安静、更向内心沉淀，同时保留了乐队一贯的温度。

items.body:
Picking up where 2024's 'Trash Can Lamb' left off, Keith Freund blurs the line between acoustic instrumentation and DIY electronics on his latest full-length, unraveling his gentle, jazzy sessions with 8-bit beats and oddball FX.

Since the beginning, Freund has been fixated on the character of a sound rather than what that sound, on its own, might represent. His piano parts rarely come off as if they've been played by hand; after chopping them to shreds, he inevitably reconstitutes them into player-piano style impossible sequences, re-organizing the notes and re-sculpting the tone completely. On 'Over Sidewalk Bryum', for example, it's the piano that provides the track's rhythm, accented by radio interference and bit-crushed oscillations. And although Freund does less chipping at his horn parts, letting the sax soar over the chattering electronics, it's still subtly tweaked - nothing's ever quite what it seems.

A swamp of discarded blips and glitches help prop up 'I'll Find a Place for Us', and Freund's soft woodwind tones make their way through the noise initially - or at least that's what we're supposed to think. In time, Freund's sax emerges and the soft-hued, woodwind-like sound is revealed to be a red herring. But that's the kind of sleight of hand that Freund seems to revel in, creating glitchy, unstable music from soft, placid sound sources, not the harsh digital detritus you'd expect to find on a Mille Plateaux disc.
items._cn_summary: Keith Freund 的新作延续了前作的探索方向，在声学乐器与DIY电子之间构建模糊地带。钢琴被采样、切碎并重组为自动钢琴式的不可能序列，成为节奏骨架，叠加无线电干扰与比特率压缩振荡；萨克斯部分则保留更多即兴呼吸感，但同样经过微妙处理，在嘈杂的故障声响中穿行。作品刻意制造听觉错觉，如以柔和木管音色引入，随后揭示其并非真实乐器，展现了对声音本体与感知之间关系的持续兴趣。整体上，专辑从平静的声响源头衍生出不稳定、充满毛刺的电子肌理，而非依赖生硬的数字噪音，体现出一种独特的错位与重组美学。

items.body:
Recorded last year, 'Lynboril Linsinopril' is a lengthy session from seasoned improvisers Adam Bohmen (on strings and amplified objects), Sue Lynch (on woodwind) and Crystabel Efemena Riley (on percussion).

All members of London's Horse Improvised Music Club, Bohmen, Lynch and Riley are motivated by the act of playing, something that's evident immediately. There's a refreshing freedom to their approach; it's relatively straightforward free improv gear, with Riley's tuff rhythm section providing an anchor for her collaborators' wildest skronk-y expressions, but breathes outside of the usual boundaries, never falling into the expected locked grooves. If you follow Cafe Oto's orbiting improv scene, this'll be worth a closer look.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是三位伦敦即兴乐手的长篇合作录音，以弦乐、放大物件、木管与打击乐展开。演奏本身即是驱动力，呈现出自由的即兴结构：打击乐提供坚实的节奏锚点，其他乐器在其上释放尖锐而嘈杂的表达，但整体并未落入常见的固定律动，而是在常规自由即兴框架之外呼吸。作品保持了即兴音乐应有的开放性与不可预测性，同时体现出演奏者之间紧密的互动意识。对于关注伦敦 Cafe Oto 周边即兴场景的听众而言，这是一次值得留意的现场式记录。

items.body:
Thee darkest, weirdest dub perennial from Keith Hudson, 1979, blooms on vinyl for first time in years, ready to scatter smoke and minds into the late and early hours...

First released in 1979 and highly in-demand ever since, the dub sibling to Keith Hudson’s ‘Nuh Skin Up’ pushes that album’s already stark blooz and The Soul Syndicate’s deadly riddims hard into the echo chamber with a balance of experimental nous and heads-down grooves that has assured its place in the pantheon of the most haunting dubs. 

Out of print for decades until a 2007 pressing spiked it back in the water table, the album firmly holds up nearly a half century since its original release on the basis of a future proofed minimalism that continues to haunt successive generations with its bony percussion and a dematerialised soul exemplary of dub metaphysics at its transcendant best.

Up there with the likes of Lee ‘Scratch’ Perry in terms of his dual role as songwriter and desk-tweaking dub maverick, Hudson really gets inside his own tunes, and The Soul Syndicate’s instrumentals, with the uncanniest insight, turning the likes of its title corker into clouds of pillowy steppers bass and streaking echoic contrails.

The way he inverts the vocals on ‘Ire Ire’ to sound properly wrong-end-of-telescope against the foregrounded crack of congas and spectral organ is just magic, and lays the groundwork for so much dub experimentation to come from the likes of everyone from Rhythm & Sound to Tricky, along with the likes of his spellbinding, skeletal steppers dub masterwork ‘Troubles’.
items._cn_summary: Keith Hudson与Soul Syndicate于1979年合作的这张dub专辑，将原曲中冷峻的布鲁斯质感与乐队致命的节奏推入深邃的回声空间，在实验性与沉稳律动之间取得平衡。作品以骨感打击乐和去物质化的人声处理为核心，呈现出一种超越性的极简主义。Hudson兼具词曲作者与混音师的双重身份，对声音细节有异常敏锐的掌控，例如在《Ire Ire》中倒置人声，使其仿佛从望远镜错误一端传来，与前景化的康加鼓和幽灵般的风琴形成奇异对比。专辑中的《Troubles》等曲目奠定了后续dub实验的范式，影响波及Rhythm & Sound与Tricky等众多音乐人。尽管问世近半世纪，其前卫的声响设计仍保持着持续的渗透力。

items.album: Music To Watch Seeds Grow By 010: KiF PRODUCTIONS (Passiflora)

items.body:
Mu-inspired space cadets KiF Productions livicate their play of Japanese environmental ambient electronics, Hassellian 4th world, the KLF’s ‘Chill Out’, and Eno-esque harmonic perfumes, to the dearly departed Keith McIvor​.

"Passiflora (Passifloraceae) is a genus of around 550 species of flowering plants, native to the tropical and subtropical Americas. The Passion Flower is a plant of improbable beauty - its blooms almost too intricate to be real, its climbing habit a quiet kind of determination. It has been used for centuries as a remedy for anxiety and sleeplessness, something that slows us and the world around us down.

Fresh from last year's triumphant debut by KiF; Still Out, Passiflora, the album, follows the plant from its very beginning. It opens in darkness - 'Secret of the Seed', dormant, waiting - before the first tentative stir of 'First Movement' and the long, instinctive reach of 'Seeking Light'. From there, the journey unfolds with the patience of something that has no choice but to grow: drinking, climbing, flowering. 'Song of the Vine' carries the plant's quiet insistence upward, while 'Florescence' and 'Pollination Dream' catch it at its most open - that brief, extraordinary moment of full bloom. Then the turn. 'Fruiting (Slight Return)' and finally 'Return to Earth' - the cycle completing itself, giving back what it always borrowed.

Each track is a stage. The whole is a life cycle."
items._cn_summary: 专辑以西番莲的生命周期为叙事结构，从种子的休眠、萌芽、向光攀爬，到开花、授粉、结果与回归大地，每首曲目对应一个生长阶段。声响构建延续了日本环境电子与哈塞尔式第四世界音乐的脉络，并融入《Chill Out》式的松弛叙事和伊诺式和谐泛音，整体呈现缓慢、耐心、有机的听觉过程。作品刻意放慢节奏，让声音像植物一样自行展开，听者仿佛在声场中观察一次完整的生命循环。适合偏好氛围化声响与自然意象结合的听众。

items.body:
Roping in Pierre Bastien and Mark Cunningham to provide brass, Mike Cooper turns in his most kaleidoscopic fourth world dream sequence to date, drawing on dub and exotica to harmonise with Andrew Pekler's marooned soundscapes...

Cooper admits in the liner notes that although he's often compared with Jon Hassell, it's German painter Mati Klarwein fantastical album covers that always reminded him exactly why he was doing what he was doing. Because Cooper makes music for imaginary places, not tangible soundtracks but half dreamed, half lived experiences that course through his catalog of experiments. And his process has never been quite so vivid as it is on 'Stochastic Parrot', a suite of vertiginous reverberations that are struck through with Cooper's "real and virtual" lap steel twangs, collaged together from samples and field recordings that wobble like heat haze. 

Different pockets of rhythm bash into each other on 'ARCHAEOPTERYX', accompanied by Bastien and Cunningham's spiraling brass improvisations. And Cooper holds the sounds together with his lulling repeated phrases; the hand drums might sound as if they're in conflict with the cycling drum machine crashes, but that's the point - it's not like channeling a dream so much as it's like being subjected to three or four dreams simultaneously. It's the ghosts of jazz fusion being raked over coals at midnight: just tune into 'SUMATRA SAMPHIRE', with its distant animalistic wails and popcorn drums, or the granulized 'HAT YAI', that sounds like the prelude to a druggy ritual.
items._genre: fourth world / experimental / dub / exotica / ambient
items._cn_summary: Mike Cooper 邀请 Pierre Bastien 与 Mark Cunningham 加入铜管演奏，以采样、田野录音与实虚滑棒吉他构建出一张第四世界风格的梦境拼贴。专辑在 dub 与异域风情之间游走，节奏层次彼此碰撞，手鼓与鼓机循环形成多重梦境同时涌入的恍惚感。Bastien 与 Cunningham 的螺旋式铜管即兴穿插其中，与 Cooper 重复的吟诵式乐句共同维系整体氛围。部分曲目如《SUMATRA SAMPHIRE》融入遥远的动物嘶吼与爆裂鼓点，《HAT YAI》则呈现颗粒化处理，带有仪式前奏般的迷幻气质。Cooper 在内页中提及，常被与 Jon Hassell 比较，但真正提醒他创作初衷的是画家 Mati Klarwein 的奇幻封面——他为想象之地而非具体场景作乐，使这张专辑介于半梦半醒的经验之间，充满热浪般摇曳的声响质感。
